TCP and IP.model: IP routes best-effort packets between interfaces. TCP turns that unreliable packet service into an ordered byte stream between endpoints; it does not preserve application message boundaries.
concepts: A subnet and routing table select the next hop; ARP or IPv6 neighbor discovery resolves the local link destination. A private address is not necessarily unique beyond its network.
TCP uses sequence numbers, acknowledgments, retransmission, flow control, and congestion control. SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK establishes state; FIN and RST have different meanings.

An endpoint is address plus port and transport. UDP preserves datagrams without TCP's delivery guarantees. A listening port, completed connection, and healthy application are three different observations.
TCP and IP.exercise: Start a loopback HTTP server, capture its traffic, and request a file twice. Identify the TCP handshake, application bytes, and close; then stop the listener and distinguish refusal from a timeout. Expected evidence: a packet trace annotated with endpoints and state transitions.
TCP and IP.quick: Windows: `Test-NetConnection 127.0.0.1 -Port 8000`; Linux: `ss -lntp` and `ip route`. A successful TCP connect proves transport reachability, not authentication or application health.
TCP and IP.risk: Exposed listeners, unauthenticated application protocols, and overbroad routing turn network reachability into an attack surface. Source IP alone is not a trustworthy user identity.
TCP and IP.test: Bind the lab server to loopback, then verify a second lab VM cannot reach it; deliberately bind to the lab interface and compare. Expected difference: only the explicitly exposed interface accepts connections.
TCP and IP.defense: Bind narrowly, allow only required network paths, authenticate at the application layer, and encrypt sensitive traffic. Monitor unexpected listeners, denied connections, unusual connection rates, and application failures together.
TCP and IP.gotcha: A TCP read may return part of a message or several messages. NAT and proxies change visible addresses; firewalls may silently drop rather than reject packets.

DNS.model: A stub resolver asks a recursive resolver, which follows delegations to authoritative servers and caches answers. DNS maps names to typed records, not just names to one IP address.
concepts: A/AAAA map addresses; CNAME aliases; NS delegates; MX, TXT, and SRV carry service-specific information. TTL bounds cache lifetime, including separately defined negative caching.

Both UDP and TCP port 53 carry normal DNS. Truncated UDP responses can require TCP; zone transfers also use TCP. Root service has 13 named identities with many anycast instances, not 13 physical servers.
DNSSEC authenticates signed data and denial of existence; it does not encrypt queries. DoT and DoH encrypt the resolver transport, which is a different trust boundary.
DNS.exercise: Run `Resolve-DnsName example.com -Type A` and repeat with `-Type AAAA` and `-Type NS`. Compare answers from your configured resolver with the authoritative delegation. Record record type, TTL, resolver, and whether each observation was cached.
DNS.quick: `Resolve-DnsName example.com -Type A`; `dig example.com A`; `dig +tcp example.com A`. Distinguish NXDOMAIN, NOERROR with no relevant answers, and SERVFAIL.
DNS.risk: Incorrect delegation, dangling service records, open recursion, and unvalidated answers can misdirect clients or expose infrastructure. DNS control is separate from ownership of an application account.
DNS.test: In a local test zone, change one A record and compare responses before and after its TTL expires. Verify that an unauthorized client cannot update the zone or perform a transfer; do not probe third-party zones.
DNS.defense: Restrict recursion, updates, and zone transfers; protect registrar and DNS-provider accounts with MFA; retire dangling records. Validate DNSSEC where supported and monitor delegation, NS, and critical application-record changes.
DNS.gotcha: A CNAME does not redirect HTTP. Cached answers can persist until TTL expiry; changing a record does not instantly change every client's view.

TLS and PKI.model: TLS establishes an authenticated, encrypted channel. PKI binds a public key to an identity through a chain of certificates rooted in a locally trusted authority.
concepts: Validate the certificate chain, validity period, intended usage, and requested hostname. Possession of any trusted certificate does not authenticate every hostname.

TLS 1.3 negotiates parameters and derives traffic keys from a handshake; the server proves possession of the certificate key. mTLS additionally authenticates a client certificate, but the application must still authorize that identity.
SNI selects a virtual host and ALPN selects an application protocol. A reverse proxy that terminates TLS creates a new trust boundary; the backend hop may have different protection.
TLS and PKI.exercise: Run a local HTTPS service with a development CA. Compare a matching hostname, a mismatched hostname, and an untrusted CA using a normal client. Expected result: only the trusted matching identity succeeds without bypass flags.
TLS and PKI.quick: `curl -v https://example.com/` exposes handshake and certificate diagnostics. Never turn `-k`/certificate-validation bypass into an application fix. Prefer TLS 1.2/1.3 with current library defaults.
TLS and PKI.risk: Disabling identity checks, trusting an inappropriate CA, exposing private keys, or assuming frontend TLS protects the backend permits impersonation or sensitive-data exposure.
TLS and PKI.test: Use the lab's wrong-hostname certificate and confirm the client refuses it. Repeat through the reverse proxy and verify both client-to-proxy and proxy-to-origin validation independently.
TLS and PKI.defense: Keep validation enabled, automate certificate renewal, protect private keys, inventory trust stores, and authenticate internal hops where needed. Alert on certificate expiry, unexpected issuers, TLS errors, and validation bypass configuration.
TLS and PKI.gotcha: Encryption does not make an endpoint trustworthy. TLS 1.3 early data can be replayed; do not use it for non-idempotent operations without explicit replay controls.

HTTP.model: HTTP defines request/response semantics. HTTP/1.1 serializes messages using a start line, headers, a blank line, and an optional framed body; intermediaries must agree on where each message ends.
concepts: Methods describe intent: GET is safe; PUT and DELETE are idempotent by semantics; POST is not generally idempotent. Status classes are informational, success, redirection, client error, and server error.
Host selects an authority. Content-Type describes representation; Content-Length counts octets, not characters. Transfer-Encoding participates in HTTP/1.1 framing; ambiguous framing must be rejected.
Connections can be reused across requests. Cookies, authorization, caching, redirects, and proxy-added headers are separate mechanisms; a redirect may change the authority and credential policy.
HTTP.exercise: Use `curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8000/` against a local server. Send GET and HEAD, compare headers and bodies, then request a missing path. Capture one persistent connection and label message boundaries. Expected result: explain each status and exactly how the client knows the response body ended.
HTTP.quick: `curl -i URL` includes response headers; `curl -v URL` shows request diagnostics; `curl -I URL` sends HEAD. A 401 requests authentication; a 403 refuses the request. JSON can be any JSON value, not only an object.
HTTP.risk: Parser disagreement, trusted client-supplied proxy headers, and missing per-request authorization let an intermediary and application interpret the same bytes differently.
HTTP.test: On a disposable reverse-proxy/backend pair, submit conflicting framing only inside the isolated lab and confirm rejection at the edge. Separately send an unexpected Host value and verify it cannot influence a password-reset URL.
HTTP.defense: Reject ambiguous framing, normalize routing at a trusted edge, configure trusted proxy hops, allowlist public authorities, and authorize each resource operation. Correlate proxy and origin request IDs when investigating mismatched responses.
HTTP.gotcha: A 200 response may contain an application error. HEAD is not GET with a body discarded by the client; its response has no content. Header names are case-insensitive, but individual field values have their own rules.

HTTP2 and HTTP3.model: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 retain HTTP semantics while changing framing and transport. HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over TCP; HTTP/3 maps streams onto QUIC over UDP.
concepts: HTTP/2 uses binary frames, stream identifiers, flow control, and HPACK header compression. Pseudo-headers such as :method and :authority replace parts of the HTTP/1.1 start line.

QUIC integrates TLS and independent reliable streams; HTTP/3 uses QPACK for header compression. TCP packet loss can stall all HTTP/2 streams on that connection, while QUIC avoids transport-level cross-stream head-of-line blocking.
ALPN and deployment policy determine the selected protocol; HTTP/3 may be advertised with Alt-Svc or HTTPS records. A proxy can accept HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 and forward HTTP/1.1 to an origin.
HTTP2 and HTTP3.exercise: Inspect the browser Network protocol column for a test HTTPS server and compare with `curl --http2 -I` where supported. Disable UDP only in a disposable lab and observe HTTP/3 fallback. Expected evidence: negotiated protocol and behavior, not an assumption based on the URL scheme.
HTTP2 and HTTP3.quick: Check `curl --version` for HTTP2/HTTP3 support before using flags. One connection can contain many streams; stream-level errors and connection-level errors have different blast radii.
HTTP2 and HTTP3.risk: Protocol translation, malformed pseudo-headers, and insufficient stream/resource limits can create parser discrepancies or denial-of-service conditions at intermediaries.
HTTP2 and HTTP3.test: Use a maintained HTTP/2 test client on your local proxy to send an invalid pseudo-header ordering and verify rejection. Compare the accepted authority and path at the edge and origin without generating high traffic.
HTTP2 and HTTP3.defense: Patch protocol implementations, enforce header/stream/time limits, reject invalid messages before downgrade, and test edge-to-origin normalization. Track resets, stream counts, CPU, and timeout rates rather than only TCP connection counts.
HTTP2 and HTTP3.gotcha: HTTP/2 support at the client-facing edge does not prove end-to-end HTTP/2. QUIC's independent streams do not remove all application-level dependencies or congestion effects.

URLs and Encoding.model: A URL is parsed into structured components before each component is decoded or interpreted. Security depends on all components using compatible parsing and normalization rules.
concepts: Distinguish scheme, authority, hostname, port, path, query, and fragment. The fragment is not sent in an ordinary HTTP request; query syntax is application-defined.

Percent encoding represents bytes. Form encoding maps plus to space, while a plus in an arbitrary path is not a space. Unicode normalization and internationalized hostnames add separate transformations.
A proxy, router, framework, and filesystem may each normalize or decode. Repeated decoding can turn previously inert percent signs into separators; canonicalize once at the relevant boundary.
URLs and Encoding.exercise: In a browser console, inspect `new URL('https://example.com/a%2Fb?q=a+b#section')`. Compare pathname, searchParams, and hash with a local server's logged request target. Expected result: explain which component changes and which never reaches the server.
URLs and Encoding.quick: Use `URL` and `URLSearchParams`, not substring checks, for URL decisions. `encodeURIComponent` encodes a component; it is not an HTML escaper or a complete URL-policy validator.
URLs and Encoding.risk: Allowlist checks performed on a different representation than the final consumer can misclassify hosts, paths, or executable data.
URLs and Encoding.test: Send a harmless path marker with single and double percent encoding through a local proxy and app. Record the value at each hop and require one unambiguous interpretation before filesystem or outbound-request use.
URLs and Encoding.defense: Use structured parsers, allowlist supported schemes and destinations, validate canonical values, and apply context-specific output encoding. Log both original request identifiers and normalized routing decisions without logging secrets.
URLs and Encoding.gotcha: Decoding is not sanitization. A string that is safe in a URL component can still be unsafe in HTML, JavaScript, SQL, or a shell.

Browser Security Model.model: The browser mediates origins, sites, ambient credentials, and access to privileged APIs. Same-origin policy primarily limits cross-origin reads; it does not prevent every cross-origin request.
concepts: An origin is scheme, host, and port. A schemeful site is a broader registrable-domain boundary used by mechanisms such as SameSite cookies; subdomains can be same-site but cross-origin.

CORS grants selected cross-origin script reads; credentialed responses require an explicit allowed origin. Cookie Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite constrain different behaviors. CSP limits selected resource and script execution sources.
Sandboxed frames, secure contexts, permissions, and navigation rules add boundaries. HTML forms and image loads demonstrate why blocked reads do not imply that no request was sent.
Browser Security Model.exercise: Run two loopback origins on different ports. Compare fetch without CORS, a permitted origin, and a denied origin; inspect server logs as well as the console. Set an HttpOnly cookie and confirm it is sent where appropriate but absent from document.cookie.
Browser Security Model.quick: SOP is a read boundary; CORS is an opt-in relaxation; CSRF concerns unwanted authenticated actions. Secure protects cookie transport, HttpOnly blocks script reads, and SameSite limits selected cross-site sending.
Browser Security Model.risk: Confusing origin with site, reflecting arbitrary origins, trusting frame messages, or relying on CSP as the sole XSS defense leaves independent trust boundaries unprotected.
Browser Security Model.test: From the second lab origin, attempt a credentialed read and a simple state-changing form request against a synthetic account. Expected result: read access is denied and the action separately requires valid CSRF protection.
Browser Security Model.defense: Use explicit CORS allowlists, appropriate cookie attributes, CSRF defenses, contextual encoding, and a restrictive tested CSP. Monitor CSP reports and suspicious origin patterns, but do not treat client-reported telemetry as authoritative.
Browser Security Model.gotcha: CORS is not authentication or server-side authorization. HttpOnly does not stop an XSS payload from acting with the victim's session through browser requests.

Linux CLI.model: A shell parses command text, starts processes, and connects byte streams. Filesystem permissions and process credentials determine what those processes can actually access.
concepts: Standard input, output, and error are distinct streams. Pipes carry stdout; exit status conveys success conventions. Quote variable expansions and understand globbing before passing filenames to utilities.
Owner/group/other mode bits and directory traversal permissions differ from file permissions. Processes have identities, environment variables, working directories, and open file descriptors.
Use pwd, ls, stat, find, grep/rg, ps, ss, and package-manager documentation to inspect state. The shell's parsing happens before an executable receives its argument vector.
Linux CLI.exercise: Create a disposable directory with filenames containing spaces. Inspect it with `find`, compare quoted and unquoted variable expansion, and redirect stdout and stderr separately. Expected evidence: exact arguments and permissions, with no work outside the disposable directory.
Linux CLI.quick: `pwd`; `id`; `stat file`; `ps -ef`; `ss -lntp`; `command --help`. Use `--` when a utility supports an end-of-options separator and an untrusted filename could begin with a dash.
Linux CLI.risk: Shell interpretation, unsafe temporary files, excessive privileges, and writable executable search paths can convert ordinary automation into unintended command execution or data exposure.
Linux CLI.test: Pass a harmless string containing spaces and semicolons to a local helper using a structured argument API, then compare it with a deliberately vulnerable toy shell wrapper. Verify the safe version treats the string as one data argument.
Linux CLI.defense: Avoid shell construction for untrusted input, use least privilege, create temporary files securely, and use explicit executable paths for sensitive automation. Audit unexpected child processes and permission changes.
Linux CLI.gotcha: Shell syntax is not portable across Bash, POSIX sh, and PowerShell. `sudo` does not make an unsafe command safe; inspect expansion and target paths before privileged operations.

Git.model: Git stores content-addressed snapshots and a graph of commits. Branches and tags are references into that graph; a remote is a named synchronization endpoint, not a backup policy by itself.
concepts: The working tree, staging index, and HEAD are different states. Diff before staging, and inspect staged content before committing. Merge joins histories; rebase rewrites commit ancestry.
Fetch downloads refs and objects without merging the working branch. Pull combines fetching with integration. Ignore rules affect untracked paths; they do not remove an already tracked secret.
Each commit links a tree and parents. Rewriting a branch does not guarantee removal from clones, caches, forks, logs, or hosted artifacts; exposed credentials must be revoked.
Git.exercise: Initialize a disposable repository, make two commits, create a branch, and resolve a small merge conflict. Add a dummy secret file to ignore rules before staging and verify `git status --short` and `git check-ignore -v` agree.
Git.quick: `git status --short`; `git diff`; `git diff --cached`; `git log --oneline --graph`; `git fetch`; `git check-ignore -v path`. Keep destructive history operations out of routine troubleshooting.
Git.risk: Publishing tracked secrets, trusting unreviewed hooks or build configuration, and granting broad repository tokens can turn source collaboration into credential or supply-chain exposure.
Git.test: Track a dummy marker, then add its path to .gitignore and show it remains tracked with `git ls-files`. Remove only the disposable marker from the index and verify ignore behavior; use no real credentials.
Git.defense: Review staged diffs, enable secret scanning and branch protections, minimize automation permissions, and pin trusted build dependencies. Rotate exposed credentials first, then coordinate history cleanup where necessary.
Git.gotcha: Deleting a file in the latest commit does not delete its history. A signed commit identifies a signing key; it does not prove that the code is safe.

Web Lab Setup.model: A web lab is a disposable environment with explicit network boundaries, synthetic identities, and a repeatable reset procedure. Vulnerable applications must not inherit production credentials or public exposure.
concepts: Choose a local VM or container setup; record image versions, ports, reset commands, and synthetic accounts. Bind vulnerable listeners to 127.0.0.1 unless a deliberately isolated lab network is required.
Use a dedicated browser profile and proxy project. Install an interception CA only in that profile or lab trust store, and remove it when the lab is retired.
Container port publishing, host firewall policy, VPN routes, and application binding are distinct controls. A container alone is not a security boundary suitable for arbitrary malicious code.
Web Lab Setup.exercise: Deploy the official Juice Shop container with host binding `127.0.0.1:3000:3000`, access it through a dedicated browser profile, capture one benign request in Burp, then reset the container. Expected result: repeatable startup/reset and no listener on an unintended interface.
Web Lab Setup.quick: Inventory: target/version, host binding, browser profile, proxy listener, trust store, reset procedure, and cleanup. Use only synthetic data. Leave corporate VPN and required proxy settings unchanged.
Web Lab Setup.risk: An accidentally public vulnerable app, broadly trusted interception CA, shared production browser session, or mounted host secret turns a training setup into a real exposure.
Web Lab Setup.test: Inspect the published host address and try access from a second isolated lab VM. A loopback-only service must remain unreachable there. Confirm the normal browser profile does not trust the lab interception CA.
Web Lab Setup.defense: Use loopback or host-only networking, dedicated profiles, narrow mounts, synthetic credentials, and documented teardown. Check listeners after startup and after cleanup; do not run vulnerable targets on corporate infrastructure.
Web Lab Setup.gotcha: Container examples using `-p 3000:3000` commonly bind all interfaces. VM bridged mode exposes the guest to a different network than host-only mode.

HTML.model: HTML is parsed into a document tree; markup syntax, DOM state, and serialized source are not identical.
concepts: Use semantic elements, associated labels, and explicit form methods. Browser validation improves usability but cannot enforce server-side rules.
Attributes, text nodes, URLs, and script blocks are distinct parsing contexts. Character references and parser error recovery can change interpretation.
The HTML parser constructs nodes while resource discovery can initiate network requests. Scripts and DOM APIs can subsequently mutate the tree.
HTML.exercise: Build a local labeled form with required fields and inspect the resulting request. Disable client validation and submit again; document why the server must validate independently.
HTML.quick: Prefer textContent for text, explicit input types, and semantic controls. Inspect the live DOM as well as View Source.
HTML.risk: Untrusted markup inserted into an executable HTML context can become XSS; trusting form constraints lets crafted requests bypass validation.
HTML.test: Render the harmless marker `LAB` once as text and once as HTML in a toy page. The safe text path must display the brackets literally.
HTML.defense: Encode for the output context, sanitize intentionally supported rich HTML with a maintained library, validate inputs server-side, and restrict framing with CSP frame-ancestors. Monitor CSP violations as supporting evidence.
HTML.gotcha: HTML escaping is not JavaScript-string escaping. A hidden input is fully attacker-controlled request data.

CSS.model: CSS computes presentation through the cascade, inheritance, selector matching, and layout; it can also cause resource loads.
concepts: Origin, importance, cascade layers, specificity, and source order participate in conflict resolution. Not every property inherits.
Flexbox handles one-dimensional alignment; Grid handles two-dimensional tracks. Use stable dimensions and content-aware breakpoints.
Style calculation feeds layout and painting. External stylesheets, fonts, and url() values can create network requests.
CSS.exercise: Build the same small toolbar with Flexbox and Grid. Inspect computed styles and overflow at narrow and wide widths; expected result: no overlapping text or shifting controls.
CSS.quick: Inspect matched and computed rules separately. Prefer minmax(), gap, and explicit overflow handling over position-based layout patches.
CSS.risk: Untrusted style rules can hide controls, alter trusted UI, and sometimes cause data-dependent requests; CSS injection is not equivalent to harmless formatting.
CSS.test: Allow only a small color-token set in a toy editor and submit a url() value. Confirm rejection and absence of an outbound resource request.
CSS.defense: Do not accept arbitrary stylesheets from untrusted users; allowlist bounded design tokens and apply CSP style-src and resource restrictions. Inspect unexpected style sources and network requests.
CSS.gotcha: A visually hidden element may remain focusable or accessible. CSS visibility does not implement authorization.

JavaScript.model: JavaScript evaluates values in lexical environments, uses prototype-based object lookup, and schedules asynchronous work through host-provided queues.
concepts: Prefer explicit conversions and strict equality; understand null, undefined, truthiness, and number precision. Closures retain access to lexical bindings.
Object property lookup can traverse prototypes. Modules provide explicit imports/exports; errors propagate synchronously or through promise rejection.
Tasks execute to completion; promise reactions use the microtask queue. Async functions return promises, and await suspends that function rather than blocking the entire runtime.
JavaScript.exercise: Log synchronous statements, a resolved promise, and a zero-delay timer; predict and verify their order. Add a rejected promise and handle it explicitly.
JavaScript.quick: Use Object.hasOwn(obj, key) for own-property checks; await with try/catch for expected failures. JSON.parse parses JSON but does not validate an application's schema.
JavaScript.risk: eval-like execution, unsafe DOM sinks, prototype mutation, and coercion-based validation allow data to influence code or policy.
JavaScript.test: Pass a marker and unexpected object keys through a toy merge/validation routine. Confirm schema rejection and that Object.prototype remains unchanged.
JavaScript.defense: Avoid dynamic code evaluation, validate runtime data, use safe text sinks, and disallow prototype-sensitive keys in generic merge paths. Monitor unhandled rejections and unexpected global mutations in tests.
JavaScript.gotcha: Async does not mean parallel CPU execution. TypeScript annotations disappear at runtime and cannot replace JavaScript input validation.

TypeScript.model: TypeScript statically checks JavaScript programs and emits JavaScript. Its type system describes assumptions; external data can violate them at runtime.
concepts: Use strict mode, discriminated unions, and narrowing to represent valid states. Prefer unknown over any at external boundaries.
Generics express relationships between types; assertions tell the checker to trust the author, not to convert or validate data.
Compiler target and module settings affect emitted code and resolution. Interfaces and most type annotations are erased.
TypeScript.exercise: Define a discriminated result type and handle every case. Parse malformed JSON into unknown and validate it before use; confirm both compiler exhaustiveness and runtime rejection.
TypeScript.quick: Run `tsc --noEmit`; enable strict and consider noUncheckedIndexedAccess. Use a runtime schema at HTTP, storage, and message boundaries.
TypeScript.risk: Casting untrusted input to a trusted interface hides missing validation while giving downstream code false confidence.
TypeScript.test: Send a string where the API expects a numeric quantity despite the client's type definitions. Verify the server rejects it without relying on the client compiler.
TypeScript.defense: Validate and normalize runtime data, limit any/assertions, keep server authorization independent, and test malformed inputs. Treat generated API types as contracts to verify, not enforcement.
TypeScript.gotcha: A successful typecheck does not prove memory safety in native dependencies, correct authorization, or safe HTML rendering.

DOM and Browser APIs.model: The DOM exposes the live document as objects; browser APIs add networking, storage, navigation, and permissions with separate origin and lifetime rules.
concepts: Events travel through capture, target, and bubbling phases. Event delegation depends on the actual target and currentTarget.
Fetch separates network failures from HTTP error responses; check response.ok. localStorage persists by origin and is readable by same-origin scripts.
Mutation APIs interpret their inputs differently: textContent inserts text, while innerHTML invokes HTML parsing. Navigation and permission APIs add further policy checks.
DOM and Browser APIs.exercise: Build a local list with event delegation and fetch-backed loading. Add explicit loading, error, and empty states; verify a 404 does not masquerade as a network exception.
DOM and Browser APIs.quick: Use createElement/textContent for untrusted text; check response.ok; keep long-lived secrets out of script-readable storage when the architecture allows it.
DOM and Browser APIs.risk: Attacker-controlled URLs, storage entries, or messages reaching HTML or navigation sinks can produce DOM XSS or unsafe redirects.
DOM and Browser APIs.test: Put `LAB` in a query parameter and show it in the page using textContent. Confirm literal rendering and no extra elements in the DOM.
DOM and Browser APIs.defense: Trace sources to sinks, validate URL schemes and destinations, use safe DOM APIs, and adopt Trusted Types where supported. Test CSP and DOM mutation behavior together.
DOM and Browser APIs.gotcha: Catching a fetch exception does not handle ordinary HTTP 4xx/5xx responses. Client-side route guards do not protect server data.

React.model: React derives a UI from props and state, then reconciles rendered output. Components should keep rendering pure and synchronize external systems deliberately.
concepts: State belongs to a component position and stable keys influence identity. Derived values usually belong in rendering, not duplicated effect-managed state.
Effects synchronize external subscriptions or imperative APIs and need cleanup. Routing and data-fetching behavior depend on the chosen framework.
JSX text is escaped, but raw HTML insertion and server/client boundaries remain explicit trust decisions. Server actions and API handlers still require authorization.
React.exercise: Build a typed editable list with stable IDs, loading/error states, and an abortable fetch. Delete one row and verify neighboring input state stays attached to the correct item.
React.quick: Prefer immutable state updates and stable keys. Avoid unnecessary effects and memoization; inspect raw HTML and external URL props during review.
React.risk: dangerouslySetInnerHTML, untrusted navigation targets, or authorization enforced only by hidden components expose data or execution paths.
React.test: Render a harmless HTML marker as ordinary JSX text and verify escaping. Call a protected endpoint directly while the UI hides its button; require server denial.
React.defense: Use ordinary JSX for text, sanitize intentional rich HTML, validate URLs, and enforce authorization in server handlers. Test hydration, server actions, and direct API access separately.
React.gotcha: A component not being rendered does not make its endpoint inaccessible. Client bundles cannot contain server secrets.

Angular.model: Angular composes typed components, templates, dependency-injected services, and change detection into a browser application.
concepts: Components own view state; services encapsulate shared operations. Forms and routes structure interaction but do not authorize server requests.
Template binding applies context-dependent sanitization. Explicit trust-bypass APIs transfer responsibility to the caller.
Compiled templates are application code. HTTP interceptors, dependency injection, and route transitions affect how requests and state propagate.
Angular.exercise: Build a form-backed component with a service and a routed detail view. Verify validation feedback, server-error handling, and navigation to a nonexistent record.
Angular.quick: Prefer normal property/text binding. Audit bypassSecurityTrust APIs, direct DOM manipulation, and any dynamic template construction.
Angular.risk: Treating attacker data as trusted HTML/resource URLs or compiling untrusted templates bypasses Angular's normal safety boundaries.
Angular.test: Bind a harmless HTML marker normally and inspect sanitization. Remove the UI route guard in a local test and verify the API still rejects unauthorized access.
Angular.defense: Avoid trust-bypass APIs for untrusted data, use AOT-supported patterns, validate server inputs, and deploy CSP/Trusted Types where practical. Monitor dependency advisories and sanitizer regressions.
Angular.gotcha: Sanitization rules differ by binding context. A frontend auth service or route guard is not a server access-control mechanism.

Vue.model: Vue tracks reactive dependencies and updates component output when relevant state changes. Templates are compiled into rendering logic.
concepts: Use refs/reactive state and computed values for derived data; watchers synchronize external effects and require deliberate lifecycle handling.
Components exchange props and events; routing and shared state add application-level structure. Escaped interpolation differs from v-html.
Reactivity tracks access and mutation, while rendering batches updates. SSR adds server/client state transfer and hydration boundaries.
Vue.exercise: Build a filtered list using computed state and a child component event. Verify filtering updates without duplicated stored state and that loading failures are visible.
Vue.quick: Use text interpolation for untrusted strings; treat v-html and dynamic template compilation as security-sensitive. Keep server secrets out of serialized client state.
Vue.risk: Untrusted templates, v-html content, and unsafe URLs can escape normal text-binding protections; client-only checks cannot authorize data.
Vue.test: Display a markup marker through interpolation and confirm literal output. Request another synthetic user's record directly and require the server to reject it.
Vue.defense: Never compile untrusted templates, sanitize supported rich HTML, constrain URL schemes, and authorize API operations server-side. Test SSR state serialization for sensitive fields.
Vue.gotcha: A reactive object is not a validation boundary. HTML escaping does not make arbitrary JavaScript or URL contexts safe.

Bundlers.model: Bundlers transform a module graph into deployable assets. Development serving and production output are different products with different exposure risks.
concepts: Vite emphasizes fast development module serving; webpack provides a configurable bundling pipeline. Both rely on plugins and loaders that execute during builds.
Tree shaking, code splitting, minification, and source maps affect output and debugging. Environment substitutions can embed values directly into client assets.
Dependency resolution, transforms, and chunk generation determine which code actually ships; reviewing source alone may miss generated artifacts.
Bundlers.exercise: Build a small app and inspect its production output for module chunks, source maps, and a deliberately public marker variable. Confirm a server-only dummy value is absent.
Bundlers.quick: Inspect production artifacts, not only source. Do not expose a development server publicly; only explicitly public configuration belongs in browser bundles.
Bundlers.risk: Malicious build plugins, leaked source maps, exposed dev servers, and embedded secrets can compromise the build or disclose implementation details.
Bundlers.test: Search the built files for a synthetic secret marker and verify the release check fails if it appears. Test dev-server binding and allowed-host behavior locally.
Bundlers.defense: Pin and review plugins, isolate build credentials, bind dev servers narrowly, and apply an explicit source-map publication policy. Scan final artifacts for sensitive markers and unexpected external resources.
Bundlers.gotcha: A variable's name does not make it secret. Build-time replacement can publish a value even if its source configuration file is ignored by Git.

npm Ecosystem.model: npm resolves packages into a dependency graph and can execute lifecycle scripts during installation. The lockfile records a concrete resolution, not a guarantee of trustworthy behavior.
concepts: package.json expresses dependencies and scripts; package-lock.json pins resolved artifacts and integrity metadata. npm ci enforces lockfile consistency.
Registries, package scopes, transitive dependencies, and lifecycle scripts are separate trust surfaces. Integrity detects changed bytes, not malicious-but-intended bytes.
Installation and build scripts run with the caller's permissions and environment. Provenance helps attribute publication but does not replace review.
npm Ecosystem.exercise: Create a disposable project, install one small dependency, and compare npm install with npm ci after intentionally changing the manifest. Inspect its dependency tree and lifecycle scripts.
npm Ecosystem.quick: `npm ci`; `npm ls`; `npm audit`; inspect lockfile diffs. Use --ignore-scripts for an initial inspection when compatible, then consciously approve required build steps.
npm Ecosystem.risk: Typosquatting, dependency confusion, compromised maintainers, and install scripts can execute code before the application starts.
npm Ecosystem.test: Use a local toy package whose install script only writes a marker. Compare installation with and without scripts and confirm the expected marker behavior.
npm Ecosystem.defense: Use scoped registries, review lockfile changes, minimize CI secrets, and verify provenance where available. Triage advisories by reachable code and apply tested updates rather than blindly forcing upgrades.
npm Ecosystem.gotcha: npm audit covers known advisories, not all malicious packages. A clean audit is not proof of supply-chain safety.

WebSockets.model: WebSockets establish a long-lived bidirectional message channel after a protocol handshake; HTTP request authorization does not automatically authorize every later message.
concepts: The HTTP/1.1 upgrade handshake includes a browser Origin header. Frames carry data or control messages, and fragmentation differs from application message semantics.
Browser JavaScript uses the WebSocket API; servers manage connection identity, subscriptions, heartbeat, and reconnect behavior.
Authentication can expire while a connection remains open. Each message and subscription needs schema, size, rate, and authorization checks.
WebSockets.exercise: Build a loopback echo service with a maintained WebSocket library. Send JSON messages, malformed input, and a clean close; record connection and message-level outcomes.
WebSockets.quick: Use wss in deployment; validate Origin for browser clients; bound message sizes and queue growth. Recheck authorization when subscriptions or privileges change.
WebSockets.risk: Accepting ambient session cookies from arbitrary origins or trusting every message after connection setup enables cross-site hijacking and unauthorized operations.
WebSockets.test: Open the lab socket from a second origin and require handshake rejection. On an authorized connection, request another synthetic user's subscription and require message-level denial.
WebSockets.defense: Allowlist origins, authenticate the session, authorize each action, validate message schemas, and handle expiry/revocation. Log identity, subscription changes, denials, and abnormal disconnects without recording secrets.
WebSockets.gotcha: Ordinary CORS response headers do not substitute for WebSocket Origin validation. Nonbrowser clients can forge Origin, so it is not authentication.

postMessage.model: postMessage transfers structured data across window boundaries that direct DOM access may not cross. The receiver must establish who sent the message and what the message is allowed to request.
concepts: targetOrigin restricts the intended destination origin; avoid wildcard delivery of sensitive data.
Check event.origin and, where appropriate, event.source against the expected window. Validate message shape, operation, and value ranges.
Structured clone copies supported values but is not a schema validator. A popup or frame may navigate between obtaining its reference and delivering later messages.
postMessage.exercise: Create a parent and iframe on different loopback origins. Exchange a versioned message with an explicit targetOrigin and verify origin/source checks before updating text.
postMessage.quick: Validate origin, source, schema, and requested action independently. Insert received text with textContent, not HTML parsing.
postMessage.risk: Wildcard sending or receivers that trust any origin can disclose data or let another window invoke privileged actions.
postMessage.test: Send a valid-looking message from an unexpected third lab origin. The receiver must ignore it and leave state unchanged; capture a diagnostic rejection without including sensitive data.
postMessage.defense: Use exact origin comparisons and expected window references, version the schema, and authorize operations. Avoid substring hostname checks and dynamic execution of received strings.
postMessage.gotcha: Checking only event.source is insufficient if that window can navigate. Checking only a payload's claimed origin trusts attacker-controlled data.

Service Workers.model: A service worker is an origin-scoped background script that can intercept requests from controlled clients and manage offline resources across page lifetimes.
concepts: Registration scope limits controlled paths; install, waiting, activate, and control are different lifecycle stages.
Fetch handlers choose network/cache strategies. Cache Storage is explicit application storage, separate from normal HTTP cache behavior.
Workers generally require secure contexts, with localhost development exceptions. Update and activation choices determine which script controls existing clients.
Service Workers.exercise: Add offline caching to a local app, then publish a new cache version. Verify online, offline, reload, and update behavior; delete old caches during controlled activation.
Service Workers.quick: Inspect registrations and Cache Storage in browser developer tools. Version cache names and avoid caching authenticated responses as public resources.
Service Workers.risk: An untrusted worker script or unsafe cache policy can persistently alter responses within its scope and expose data across application sessions.
Service Workers.test: Log in as two synthetic users in the lab and confirm user-specific responses never appear from a shared offline cache after logout or account switching.
Service Workers.defense: Serve worker code from trusted controlled paths, constrain scope, define explicit caching rules, and test update/cleanup behavior. Monitor unexpected registrations and stale response versions.
Service Workers.gotcha: Closing a tab does not necessarily unregister the worker. Clearing ordinary HTTP cache may not remove Cache Storage or registrations.

WebAssembly.model: WebAssembly executes validated modules in a host sandbox; imports expose capabilities, while linear memory represents a module-managed byte-addressable region.
concepts: Modules declare imports and exports; instantiation supplies host functions, memory, and other required objects.
Linear-memory bounds checks protect the host boundary, but native-language bugs can still corrupt logical objects inside that memory.
JavaScript bridges strings, buffers, and errors across the module interface. The sandbox does not make exposed host imports safe or enforce application authorization.
WebAssembly.exercise: Compile a tiny arithmetic function with an established toolchain and call its export from JavaScript. Inspect memory and test invalid input and an out-of-bounds access in the toy module.
WebAssembly.quick: Review imports as a capability list; validate lengths and encodings at the host/module boundary. A trap is not a substitute for application validation.
WebAssembly.risk: Excessive host capabilities, unsafe buffer handling, and treating opaque compiled code as trusted can undermine the intended sandbox boundary.
WebAssembly.test: Instantiate the lab module with a minimal import object and verify that an undeclared or missing privileged import cannot be used. Bound execution/input size to avoid a frozen page.
WebAssembly.defense: Limit imports, validate interfaces, use memory-safe source where practical, and isolate expensive work in workers. Track traps and unexpected resource consumption.
WebAssembly.gotcha: Wasm is not encryption or a secret-storage mechanism. Downloaded modules and their embedded constants can be inspected.

x64 Assembly and Windows ABI.model: Assembly expresses machine operations; the Windows x64 ABI defines the contract that lets separately compiled functions exchange arguments, preserve state, and unwind.
concepts: Integer/pointer arguments in positions one through four use RCX, RDX, R8, R9; floating arguments use XMM0 through XMM3 by position. Later arguments are stack-passed.
The caller reserves 32 bytes of shadow space. Maintain required 16-byte stack alignment outside prolog/epilog exceptions; CALL's pushed return address matters when examining entry state.

RAX normally carries scalar integer returns. RBX, RBP, RSI, RDI, R12-R15 and XMM6-XMM15 are nonvolatile in the baseline ABI; unwind metadata describes nonleaf stack restoration. Inspect flags and operand widths when interpreting branches.
x64 Assembly and Windows ABI.exercise: Compile a small function with mixed integer/floating arguments and one stack argument using MSVC. Inspect its disassembly and unwind information; annotate each argument location, stack adjustment, and preserved register.
x64 Assembly and Windows ABI.quick: Argument position, not separate integer/float counters, selects the first four register slots. Track operand size, signedness, flags, shadow space, and alignment together.
x64 Assembly and Windows ABI.risk: Incorrect signatures, stack alignment, register preservation, or unwind metadata can corrupt state and make native interop exploitable or unreliable.
x64 Assembly and Windows ABI.test: Call a toy function through the correct declared signature and compare with compiler diagnostics for a mismatched declaration. Use a disposable process; do not patch system code.
x64 Assembly and Windows ABI.defense: Use matching headers and supported interop definitions, compiler diagnostics, stack protection, and sanitizers where supported. Investigate crashes with disassembly and the centralized WinDbg reference.
x64 Assembly and Windows ABI.gotcha: Windows x64 is not the System V AMD64 ABI. Varargs, aggregates, vectors, and newer ABI extensions have additional rules; check current Microsoft documentation.

C and CPP on Windows.model: MSVC compiles source into object files and links them with libraries into PE images; runtime behavior depends on native object lifetime, ABI, and resource ownership.
concepts: Separate compilation, linking, runtime library selection, and architecture targets. Keep declarations, calling conventions, and binary dependencies compatible.
Use RAII for handles and memory in C++; in C, make ownership and cleanup paths explicit. Pointer validity, bounds, and integer conversions are independent concerns.
Debug symbols map machine code to source; optimization can reorder or remove source-level constructs. Compiler warnings and static analysis catch only part of runtime misuse.
C and CPP on Windows.exercise: Build a small Unicode file reader with MSVC, explicit length checks, and deterministic cleanup. Test an empty file, missing file, and oversized input; inspect the PE and symbols.
C and CPP on Windows.quick: Use the Developer Command Prompt; enable high warnings and relevant analysis. Match allocator/deallocator families and check API return values before consuming outputs.
C and CPP on Windows.risk: Buffer misuse, use-after-free, unchecked arithmetic, and mismatched ownership can turn input processing into memory corruption.
C and CPP on Windows.test: Run malformed and boundary-length inputs through the toy reader with supported AddressSanitizer settings. Expected result: clean rejection or a diagnostic that identifies the defect.
C and CPP on Windows.defense: Prefer bounded abstractions and RAII, validate sizes before allocation/copy, enable compiler mitigations, and test error paths. Retain symbols for crash triage without exposing private source unnecessarily.
C and CPP on Windows.gotcha: The Windows LLP64 model keeps long at 32 bits on x64. sizeof(pointer) is not the size of the pointed-to allocation.

Windows Architecture Overview.model: Windows combines user-mode subsystems and services with a kernel-mode executive, low-level kernel, hardware abstraction, and drivers. Privilege boundaries matter more than component naming.
concepts: User applications call Win32 APIs; implementations may cross through Native API/system-call interfaces. Services remain user-mode unless a separate driver performs kernel work.
The executive manages processes, memory, objects, security, configuration, and I/O. The kernel handles low-level scheduling, interrupts, synchronization, and exception machinery.
Sessions, logon identities, processes, threads, and object namespaces are different scopes. Drivers execute with substantial trust; a bug in a driver can affect the whole system.
Windows Architecture Overview.exercise: In a Windows VM, map a test application, its service dependency, loaded modules, and device interactions using Sysinternals. Produce a diagram labeling user/kernel and identity boundaries without adding page-table material.
Windows Architecture Overview.quick: Distinguish API contract from implementation, service from driver, and process identity from the effective thread token. Use public symbols and documented interfaces for observations.
Windows Architecture Overview.risk: Confusing component boundaries leads to incorrect assumptions about who validates input, which identity authorizes access, and which code runs with kernel privilege.
Windows Architecture Overview.test: Run the same harmless resource access under standard and elevated synthetic lab users; compare access decisions and relevant object permissions instead of assuming elevation bypasses every control.
Windows Architecture Overview.defense: Apply least privilege at each interface, restrict driver installation, retain platform protections, and correlate process, token, service, and driver telemetry during investigation.
Windows Architecture Overview.gotcha: Architecture diagrams describe relationships, not a stable private API. Internal structures and implementation details change across Windows builds.

Windows Tooling Setup.model: A reproducible toolchain gives multiple independent views of the same Windows state: process inspection, event capture, disassembly, and debugging.
concepts: Obtain Sysinternals, System Informer, x64dbg, and Ghidra/IDA from official sources; record versions and signatures/hashes where published.
Use Sysinternals/System Informer for live state, x64dbg for user-mode debugging, and Ghidra/IDA for static analysis. See WinDbg for its setup and commands only.
Symbols and matching binaries determine the quality of names and types. Elevated tool access changes visibility and risk; use it only when the observation requires it.
Windows Tooling Setup.exercise: Build a harmless executable and inspect its process, open file handle, loaded modules, and one function in the chosen disassembler. Record which tool supplied each observation and whether symbols matched.
Windows Tooling Setup.quick: Keep a version inventory, clean baseline, symbol-cache location, and known-good test executable. Compare observations from at least two tools before inferring hidden behavior.
Windows Tooling Setup.risk: Untrusted tool binaries, plugins, broad elevation, or accidental execution of samples can compromise the analyst environment.
Windows Tooling Setup.test: Verify signatures or published hashes for downloaded tools and run only the self-authored sample. Confirm the analysis VM has no shared production credentials or writable sensitive mounts.
Windows Tooling Setup.defense: Use official distributions, isolate plugins, snapshot the VM, and separate static inspection from execution. Retain tool provenance and avoid disabling host protections for convenience.
Windows Tooling Setup.gotcha: A missing object may reflect access restrictions, sampling time, or tool limitations rather than concealment. Kernel-backed inspection tools add their own trusted driver surface.

Windows Lab Setup.model: Windows training needs separate disposable environments for AD, native debugging, vulnerable drivers, and potentially hostile samples; no single shared VM is appropriate for all of them.
concepts: Use host-only or internal networks for AD and vulnerable targets; document addresses, snapshots, test accounts, and reset dependencies. Avoid bridged access to corporate networks.
Keep kernel debugger host and target separate; use the WinDbg note for commands. Record matching symbols, OS build, transport, and recovery procedure.
Driver test signing and protection changes belong only in dedicated disposable targets. Malware-analysis environments need stricter network and shared-folder controls than ordinary development VMs.
Windows Lab Setup.exercise: Create clean snapshots for one ordinary Windows VM and one dedicated debug target. Verify isolation and restore a deliberately changed harmless file; document how an AD lab would be separately provisioned and reset.
Windows Lab Setup.quick: Record host/guest boundary, network mode, synthetic identities, snapshot dependency order, debugger transport, and cleanup. Keep the corporate VPN connected and unchanged.
Windows Lab Setup.risk: Shared credentials, bridged vulnerable guests, host-mounted secrets, and relaxed host protections can let a lab affect real systems.
Windows Lab Setup.test: From each lab VM, verify only explicitly intended lab peers are reachable and sensitive host shares are absent. Use harmless connectivity checks against your own endpoints only.
Windows Lab Setup.defense: Separate lab purposes, use narrow networking, synthetic accounts, trusted images, and known-good snapshots. Keep the host patched and leave its Secure Boot and endpoint protections enabled.
Windows Lab Setup.gotcha: Snapshots of interdependent domain controllers are not a substitute for understanding AD restore behavior. A kernel debugger can disrupt or crash its target.

Nodejs and Express.model: Node provides a JavaScript runtime and asynchronous I/O; Express composes ordered middleware around HTTP requests and responses.
concepts: Middleware order determines which parsers, identity checks, routes, and error handlers run. A handler must terminate the response or pass control deliberately.
Bound body size and validate parsed data; JSON parsing alone does not establish a schema. Configure proxy trust to match actual trusted hops.
CPU-heavy work blocks the event loop unless moved elsewhere. Error propagation differs between Express versions, so pin the runtime/framework and test rejected async handlers.
Nodejs and Express.exercise: Build GET and POST routes for synthetic notes with a bounded JSON parser, schema validation, and a final error handler. Verify malformed JSON, missing fields, and unknown IDs produce deliberate 4xx responses.
Nodejs and Express.quick: Keep parsing, authentication, authorization, business logic, and error mapping explicit. Use a nonprivileged runtime identity and production error responses without stack traces.
Nodejs and Express.risk: Unsafe object merging, shell construction, overtrusted forwarded headers, and missing object authorization turn untrusted request data into server authority.
Nodejs and Express.test: Call another synthetic user's note ID directly and send a forged X-Forwarded-For header. Verify resource denial and that untrusted headers cannot alter a security decision.
Nodejs and Express.defense: Validate schemas, avoid shell/eval sinks, configure trust proxy narrowly, and use per-resource authorization. Log request IDs, validation failures, and unexpected child processes without secrets.
Nodejs and Express.gotcha: Hiding a route in the UI does not protect it. An async API does not make synchronous CPU work nonblocking.

Nextjs.model: Next.js combines routing, React rendering, and server execution; every boundary where server data reaches a browser or a callable action requires deliberate policy.
concepts: App Router layouts, pages, route handlers, and server actions have different responsibilities. Server and client components determine where code runs, not whether data is authorized.
Rendering and caching defaults change across releases. Mark personalized data flows explicitly and inspect the deployed runtime rather than assuming a universal cache policy.
Server actions are externally callable operations. Serialize only safe data across the server/client boundary and keep secrets in server-only modules.
Nextjs.exercise: Build a small authenticated notes page with a server-side mutation and a detail route. Test two synthetic accounts and inspect the client bundle and network responses for unintended data.
Nextjs.quick: Authorize inside each route handler/action. Separate public cached data from per-user data; document the exact Next.js version and runtime.
Nextjs.risk: Missing action authorization, cached personalized responses, or accidental client imports can disclose server data despite a protected-looking page.
Nextjs.test: Replay a mutation directly with another synthetic identity and verify denial. Load two users' pages sequentially and confirm no personalized response is reused across them.
Nextjs.defense: Centralize data-access authorization, validate action inputs, explicitly scope caching, and scan client artifacts for dummy secret markers. Monitor action failures and unexpected cross-user access.
Nextjs.gotcha: Server-only execution does not imply trusted input. Middleware alone is not a sufficient authorization boundary for every data operation.

Python.model: Python applications combine an interpreter, imported modules, dependency environment, and server interface; framework-independent runtime choices affect every request handler.
concepts: Use isolated environments and pinned dependencies. Imports execute module-level code; package origin and search paths are part of the trust model.
Exceptions, context managers, and explicit ownership structure cleanup. Async coroutines cooperate with an event loop; blocking work needs an appropriate boundary.
WSGI describes synchronous application/server interaction; ASGI supports asynchronous protocols and lifecycles. Neither standard automatically supplies authentication or schema validation.
Python.exercise: Create a virtual environment and a small JSON-processing function with explicit validation and tests for empty, malformed, and oversized input. Confirm dependencies resolve from the intended environment.
Python.quick: `python -m venv .venv`; `python -m pip --version`; use pathlib, subprocess argument lists, and context managers instead of string-built operations.
Python.risk: eval, untrusted pickle, unsafe YAML loading, shell=True with data, and attacker-controlled import paths can execute unintended code.
Python.test: Pass a harmless shell-metacharacter string through subprocess with an argument list and shell disabled. Verify it stays data and no additional command runs.
Python.defense: Avoid dynamic evaluation and unsafe object deserialization, validate inputs, constrain imports, and isolate dependencies. Log unexpected process creation and parsing failures with size limits.
Python.gotcha: Virtual environments isolate package selection, not operating-system privileges. Async functions can still block if they call synchronous I/O.

Flask.model: Flask maps requests into view functions within application/request contexts and delegates production serving to a WSGI server.
concepts: An application factory supports configuration and testing; blueprints group routes. Request context provides per-request objects, not global user state.
Jinja templates normally escape relevant HTML output, but rendering template source from user input is a different operation. Default sessions are signed client-side data, not encrypted storage.
The development server and debugger are for development. Proxy handling, secret-key management, body limits, and production error behavior need explicit deployment choices.
Flask.exercise: Build a factory-based app with a form, signed session, and parameterized template. Use the test client for missing input, unauthorized access, and a literal HTML marker.
Flask.quick: Use render_template with fixed templates and data parameters. Keep debug disabled in deployment and avoid storing secrets in client-readable session contents.
Flask.risk: Exposed debugging, weak signing keys, untrusted template source, and absent CSRF or resource checks can compromise the application.
Flask.test: Submit a template-expression marker as ordinary form data and confirm literal output. Verify a state-changing form fails without its CSRF token in the chosen protection library.
Flask.defense: Protect secret keys, use maintained CSRF/session components, validate request data, and authorize resources. Log authentication and validation failures without exposing debugger details.
Flask.gotcha: A signed session is tamper-evident, not confidential. Flask does not add every security control automatically.

Django.model: Django integrates request middleware, views, templates, models, forms, and authentication, but application-specific object permissions remain the developer's responsibility.
concepts: Middleware order affects security, sessions, CSRF, and authentication. Forms validate submitted values; models express data constraints and persistence.
The ORM parameterizes ordinary values, while raw SQL and dynamic identifiers require separate care. Template autoescaping does not make every output context safe.
Admin, static/media serving, allowed hosts, secure cookie settings, and proxy/TLS configuration shape the deployed attack surface.
Django.exercise: Build a small model-backed form and per-user detail view. Test validation, CSRF rejection, duplicate constraints, and direct access to another user's object.
Django.quick: Run `manage.py check --deploy` against deployment settings. Keep DEBUG false, ALLOWED_HOSTS explicit, and uploaded media separate from executable application code.
Django.risk: Misconfigured deployment, unsafe template filters/raw queries, and missing object-level authorization can bypass otherwise strong framework defaults.
Django.test: Use Django's test client with CSRF enforcement enabled and two synthetic accounts. Require denial for missing tokens and cross-user object access.
Django.defense: Retain security middleware, use forms/serializers and ORM binding, define object permissions, and secure admin access. Monitor denied hosts, CSRF failures, and privileged changes.
Django.gotcha: Being authenticated or staff does not automatically imply permission to every object. Development test clients can bypass CSRF unless configured to enforce it.

FastAPI.model: FastAPI builds ASGI endpoints from typed declarations and dependencies, providing runtime request validation and generated OpenAPI while leaving policy decisions explicit.
concepts: Path/query/body declarations and Pydantic models define parsing and validation. Dependencies compose shared checks and resources.
Authentication dependencies identify callers; authorization must still check the requested object and action. Response models help constrain serialized fields.
Async handlers should avoid blocking I/O; sync dependencies/handlers have different execution behavior. ASGI deployment, worker limits, and timeouts affect availability.
FastAPI.exercise: Create a typed notes endpoint with an identity dependency and response model. Test malformed bodies, unknown IDs, unauthorized owners, and accidental internal fields.
FastAPI.quick: Use explicit request/response models and documented HTTP errors. Treat OpenAPI as a visible contract, not evidence that authorization is implemented.
FastAPI.risk: Overbroad serialization, missing dependency enforcement, permissive CORS, and blocking work in async routes can disclose data or exhaust service capacity.
FastAPI.test: Return a model containing a dummy internal field and verify the response model excludes it. Attempt a cross-user record read and require denial.
FastAPI.defense: Validate schemas, centralize identity dependencies, enforce object permissions, constrain responses, and bound request/work sizes. Monitor validation errors and endpoint latency.
FastAPI.gotcha: A Python type hint outside validated boundaries is not a runtime check. OAuth helper classes do not implement a complete identity provider.

PHP and Laravel.model: PHP executes server-side request code; Laravel layers routing, middleware, Blade templates, Eloquent persistence, and application services over that runtime.
concepts: Composer manages dependencies and autoloading. Route middleware orders session, CSRF, authentication, and other checks.
Blade escaped output differs from raw output. Eloquent query binding differs from raw expressions; mass assignment needs an explicit field policy.
Production serving, PHP-FPM/web-server configuration, writable directories, environment files, and queue workers create separate operational boundaries.
PHP and Laravel.exercise: Build a form-backed resource with a Laravel policy, request validation, and a bounded fillable field list. Verify invalid data and unauthorized updates fail.
PHP and Laravel.quick: Use escaped Blade output, policies/gates, validated request data, and bound queries. Keep APP_DEBUG false and .env outside public serving paths.
PHP and Laravel.risk: Unsafe unserialize, raw template output, arbitrary mass assignment, and exposed configuration can turn request data into execution or privilege changes.
PHP and Laravel.test: Submit an extra synthetic role field to a profile update and verify it is ignored or rejected. Confirm a markup marker renders as text and .env is not served.
PHP and Laravel.defense: Use explicit assignment schemas, policies, CSRF middleware, safe serialization, and least-privilege service identities. Monitor authorization failures and sensitive configuration access attempts.
PHP and Laravel.gotcha: Client-hidden fields are still submit-able. A web server should expose only the application's intended public directory.

Java and Spring.model: Spring Boot assembles a JVM application from dependency-injected components, configuration, web handlers, and an ordered security filter chain.
concepts: Controllers bind requests to parameters/DTOs; validation annotations require the appropriate validation integration. Services should own business invariants.
Spring Security distinguishes authentication, request authorization, CSRF, and method-level controls. Filter ordering and multiple chains can alter coverage.
Dependency resolution, application properties, Actuator exposure, template rendering, and JVM deployment settings influence the runtime boundary.
Java and Spring.exercise: Create a small REST controller with validated DTOs, a service, and object ownership checks. Test unauthenticated, wrong-owner, invalid, and valid requests.
Java and Spring.quick: Use DTOs rather than binding directly to privileged persistence entities. Expose only required Actuator endpoints and keep detailed errors out of public responses.
Java and Spring.risk: Overbinding, unsafe deserialization, expression evaluation, exposed management endpoints, and incomplete filter-chain coverage can bypass intended controls.
Java and Spring.test: Send an unexpected administrative field to a DTO and confirm rejection or exclusion. Verify management endpoints and alternate route patterns require the intended identity.
Java and Spring.defense: Constrain binding and serializers, use explicit security matchers and method/object checks, patch dependencies, and isolate management access. Monitor authentication failures and configuration/management changes.
Java and Spring.gotcha: A security annotation can be ineffective when calls bypass the expected proxy mechanism. Confirm behavior with endpoint-level tests rather than annotation presence alone.

ASP Net Core.model: ASP.NET Core routes requests through ordered middleware to controllers or minimal API handlers, with dependency injection supplying application services.
concepts: Routing, authentication, authorization, endpoint execution, and exception handling have ordering requirements. Model binding and validation are separate from resource authorization.
Use request/response DTOs, cancellation tokens, and explicit status semantics. Problem Details provides a consistent error shape without exposing internals.
Configuration providers, forwarded-header trust, hosting identity, Data Protection keys, and deployment topology affect security across application instances.
ASP Net Core.exercise: Build a small typed API with GET and POST, validation, an ownership policy, and Problem Details. Test 400, 401/403, 404, and successful creation including its Location header.
ASP Net Core.quick: Authenticate the caller, authorize the resource, validate the model, then perform the operation. Never trust arbitrary forwarded headers or expose development exception pages in production.
ASP Net Core.risk: Missing endpoint authorization, overposting, unsafe deserialization, and misconfigured proxy or key trust can expose data despite framework protections.
ASP Net Core.test: Invoke a protected endpoint directly with the wrong synthetic user and an extra privileged field. Verify denial and that response DTOs exclude dummy internal data.
ASP Net Core.defense: Apply endpoint and resource policies, constrain DTOs, secure Data Protection key storage, and use production exception handling. Log correlation IDs and authorization outcomes, not tokens.
ASP Net Core.gotcha: Authentication establishes identity; authorization establishes permission. Anti-forgery requirements differ between cookie-authenticated browser flows and bearer-token APIs.

Go.model: Go's net/http server dispatches requests to handlers, with goroutines providing concurrency and contexts carrying cancellation and deadlines.
concepts: Handlers must write deliberate status and response bodies; once headers are sent, later status changes do not replace them.
Use bounded body reads, structured decoding, and explicit validation. html/template provides contextual escaping; text/template does not provide HTML safety.
Request contexts propagate cancellation. Server timeouts, goroutine lifetime, shared-state synchronization, and connection limits affect resilience.
Go.exercise: Build a local JSON endpoint with a body limit, decoder checks, validation, and a request deadline. Test malformed input, trailing data, and client cancellation.
Go.quick: Use r.Context(), explicit http.Server timeouts, and parameterized database calls. Check every returned error and close owned resources.
Go.risk: Unbounded reads, goroutine leaks, unsafe template choice, and missing resource authorization expose availability and data boundaries.
Go.test: Submit an oversized body and confirm bounded rejection. Cancel a request to a toy slow dependency and verify its work stops rather than continuing indefinitely.
Go.defense: Bound inputs and concurrency, propagate context, use safe templates, and authorize every resource. Monitor goroutine counts, latency, timeouts, and rejected requests.
Go.gotcha: A data race is not fixed by using goroutines. The default convenience server lacks many production timeout choices you should set explicitly.

Template Engines.model: A template engine evaluates trusted template source against data. Server-side template injection occurs when untrusted input becomes part of the template program itself.
concepts: Jinja2, Twig, and Razor expose different syntax and runtime capabilities. Fixed templates with data parameters differ fundamentally from compiling user-controlled template text.
Autoescaping usually addresses selected output contexts, not server-side expression evaluation. Marking content safe bypasses an output protection, not an input validator.
Template loaders, includes, globals, helper functions, and sandbox policies determine reachable functionality. Sandboxing is engine- and version-specific.
Template Engines.exercise: Render a fixed template containing a name variable and submit literal expression syntax as the name. Verify it remains data; compare only in a separate deliberately vulnerable toy template.
Template Engines.quick: Keep template source fixed; pass values separately. Use context-aware escaping and review raw/safe helpers and dynamic include paths.
Template Engines.risk: Concatenating request data into template source can execute server-side expressions; raw output can separately introduce client-side XSS.
Template Engines.test: In an isolated toy engine, compare a harmless arithmetic expression supplied as data versus template source. The safe application must never evaluate the data value.
Template Engines.defense: Separate source from data, constrain loaders/helpers, avoid untrusted template compilation, and sanitize intentional rich output. Monitor unexpected template errors and dynamic template creation.
Template Engines.gotcha: Escaping HTML does not prevent SSTI because evaluation happens before output rendering. Different engines can share syntax while exposing very different capabilities.

Serialization.model: Serialization converts structured values to a transport/storage representation; parsing reconstructs values under a schema and trust policy chosen by the application.
concepts: JSON supports objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null at the top level. Duplicate-key and number-handling behavior can differ by parser.
XML adds namespaces, DTDs, and possible entity resolution; YAML supports richer typing and graph features. Safe data loading differs from arbitrary object construction.
Type metadata, entity resolvers, aliases, recursion, and input size affect both execution risk and resource consumption. Parsing success is not business validation.
Serialization.exercise: Parse the same small record in JSON, XML, and YAML using maintained safe APIs. Test unexpected fields, duplicate keys, invalid types, and a bounded oversized input.
Serialization.quick: Choose a minimal data format, validate schemas, disable unneeded external resolution/type construction, and cap size/depth. Do not deserialize untrusted native object graphs.
Serialization.risk: External entities, unsafe constructors, polymorphic type selection, and parser disagreement can cause file/network access, execution, or denial of service.
Serialization.test: Use a lab XML document referencing a harmless nonexistent local resource and confirm external resolution is disabled. Verify an unapproved YAML tag cannot construct an object.
Serialization.defense: Use safe loader modes and allowlisted types, disable DTD/external entities where unnecessary, and enforce size/depth limits. Monitor parse failures and unexpected parser-originated I/O.
Serialization.gotcha: A cryptographic signature establishes integrity only if correctly verified; it does not make dangerous object construction an appropriate design.

REST APIs.model: A REST-oriented HTTP API exposes resources and operations through a consistent contract; the server owns validation, authorization, and state transitions.
concepts: Use methods and status codes according to their semantics. Represent creation, missing resources, conflicts, pagination, and versioning deliberately.
Authentication identifies a caller; object-level and function-level authorization decide what that caller may read or change.
Idempotency, concurrency control, rate limits, and bounded pagination protect state and capacity. Serialization must exclude internal fields explicitly.
REST APIs.exercise: Implement a synthetic notes API with two users, pagination, and a versioned update. Test ownership, invalid input, stale updates, and repeated creation requests.
REST APIs.quick: Document request/response schemas and errors. Check actor, object, action, and tenant on every operation; use bounded page sizes and explicit writable fields.
REST APIs.risk: Broken object authorization, overposting, excessive data exposure, and unbounded operations are independent of how predictable an identifier is.
REST APIs.test: Swap one synthetic user's object ID for another's across read, update, and delete. Every unauthorized operation must fail consistently without leaking protected fields.
REST APIs.defense: Centralize resource policies, validate DTOs, constrain response fields, enforce quotas, and test an authorization matrix. Log denied object/action combinations and unusual enumeration patterns.
REST APIs.gotcha: UUIDs reduce guessability but do not authorize access. A 404 can conceal existence, but policy still must be enforced before returning data.

GraphQL.model: GraphQL executes a client-selected field tree against a schema and resolver graph; each resolver can cross a separate data and authorization boundary.
concepts: Schemas define types, queries, mutations, and inputs. Variables carry data separately from query syntax; introspection describes the schema.
Resolvers should batch efficiently without mixing users or tenants in caches. Field and object policies must match the actual returned data.
Aliases, batching, nested selections, and expensive fields influence query cost. A single HTTP request can trigger many backend operations.
GraphQL.exercise: Build a small schema with users and owned notes. Query nested fields, repeat fields with aliases, and test a denied object through every available relationship.
GraphQL.quick: Authorize in data access/resolvers, validate inputs, bound depth and cost, and scope loaders per request/identity. Introspection controls do not replace authorization.
GraphQL.risk: Resolver authorization gaps, cross-request cache reuse, and unbounded query complexity can leak data or exhaust backend resources.
GraphQL.test: Reach another synthetic user's note both directly and through a parent relationship; require identical denial. Submit a bounded over-budget query and verify controlled rejection.
GraphQL.defense: Apply object/field policies, request-scoped batching, pagination and complexity limits, and production error redaction. Log operation names, cost, denials, and resolver latency.
GraphQL.gotcha: HTTP 200 may contain GraphQL errors alongside partial data. Disabling introspection does not make an otherwise exposed schema safe.

gRPC.model: gRPC maps typed service methods onto HTTP/2, commonly using Protocol Buffers and supporting unary or streaming message exchanges.
concepts: A .proto schema defines services and field numbers. Generated clients improve contract consistency but do not validate business permissions.
Metadata carries authentication context; interceptors can apply shared checks. Deadlines and cancellation must propagate to downstream work.
Streaming changes lifetime and flow-control behavior. Bound message sizes, stream counts, and work per message; handle status codes separately from HTTP assumptions.
gRPC.exercise: Build a unary echo method and a short server stream using generated stubs. Test a deadline, cancellation, invalid identity, and an oversized message.
gRPC.quick: Set deadlines explicitly, preserve cancellation, use TLS/mTLS where appropriate, and authorize the method plus referenced resource. Never reuse retired protobuf field numbers.
