gRPC.risk: Overtrusted metadata, missing per-message/resource checks, and unbounded streams can expose data or retain work after clients disappear.
gRPC.test: Cancel a synthetic streaming call and confirm server work ends. Request another user's resource with a valid but insufficient identity and require a permission error.
gRPC.defense: Validate identity at the transport/application boundary, enforce resource policies, bound streams/messages, and use structured status handling. Monitor active streams, deadlines, cancellations, and authorization failures.
gRPC.gotcha: mTLS authenticates a certificate identity, not every requested operation. A generated client does not prevent a custom client from sending unexpected values.

Nginx.model: Nginx selects a virtual server and location, then serves a resource or proxies it to an upstream according to effective configuration and inheritance.
concepts: Server name, listening socket, and location matching jointly determine routing. Prefix and regular-expression locations have distinct selection rules.
root and alias map paths differently; proxy_pass URI handling depends on its form and location context. Validate the actual normalized path seen by the upstream.
TLS termination, buffering, upstream timeouts, forwarded headers, and inherited directives create trust and availability boundaries.
Nginx.exercise: Configure a loopback static location and a reverse-proxied toy API. Run `nginx -t`, request known and missing paths, and compare edge/origin logs for trailing-slash variants.
Nginx.quick: `nginx -t` checks configuration; inspect the effective configuration before reload. Set explicit trusted authorities, request limits, and upstream timeouts.
Nginx.risk: Path-mapping mistakes, exposed internal locations, untrusted forwarded headers, and edge/origin parsing differences can bypass intended routing controls.
Nginx.test: Try harmless dot-segment and trailing-slash variants against the isolated static/proxy setup. Verify all resolved paths remain inside the intended resource boundary.
Nginx.defense: Keep routing simple, test root/alias/proxy_pass mappings, reject unknown hosts, and set headers at trusted boundaries. Correlate edge and origin logs and patch protocol implementations.
Nginx.gotcha: Configuration syntax validity does not prove routing correctness. An alias location cannot be reasoned about as if it were a root location.

Apache.model: Apache combines virtual-host selection, modules, filesystem/directory policy, and optional proxying to decide how each request is processed.
concepts: Virtual hosts select site configuration; directory and location sections govern different namespaces. Per-directory overrides can change effective behavior.
Modules implement rewriting, authentication, proxying, and content handling. A filename extension becomes executable only when handler configuration makes it so.
Rewrite and path mapping can run at different stages; inherited permissions and AllowOverride choices determine who can change policy.
Apache.exercise: Create a local virtual host with a static directory and denied private subdirectory. Validate configuration and test direct, rewritten, and missing paths.
Apache.quick: Use `apachectl configtest` or the platform equivalent; inspect loaded modules and effective virtual hosts. Disable unneeded overrides and directory listings.
Apache.risk: Overbroad overrides, unsafe handler mappings, rewrite mistakes, and permissive proxy configuration can expose files or execute uploaded content.
Apache.test: Upload a harmless text file to a nonexecuting lab media directory and verify it remains data regardless of its extension. Confirm private paths stay denied after rewriting.
Apache.defense: Minimize modules, separate executable and upload directories, restrict AllowOverride, and define explicit access policies. Monitor handler changes, unexpected listings, and denied path variants.
Apache.gotcha: Filesystem permissions and HTTP authorization are separate checks. A Location rule and a Directory rule do not necessarily describe the same resources.

IIS.model: IIS maps bindings to sites and applications, runs workloads in application pools, and processes requests through modules, handlers, filtering, and authentication.
concepts: Application-pool identity determines resource access. Separate pools can reduce accidental cross-application access but are not a complete isolation guarantee.
Handlers choose how content executes; request filtering constrains methods, extensions, sizes, and paths. Authentication and authorization are separate modules/policies.
web.config inheritance and delegated configuration affect effective behavior. Reverse proxies and ASP.NET Core hosting add another application boundary.
IIS.exercise: Host a local static site and a toy app in separate pools. Inspect effective authentication, handler mappings, and filesystem rights; test missing and denied resources.
IIS.quick: Use explicit bindings and least-privilege pool identities. Keep upload directories nonexecuting and detailed errors restricted to local diagnostics.
IIS.risk: Overprivileged pools, unsafe handler mappings, inherited configuration surprises, and exposed diagnostics can disclose data or execute unintended content.
IIS.test: Place a harmless marker in a directory inaccessible to the pool identity and confirm the app cannot read it. Verify uploaded text is never routed to an executable handler.
IIS.defense: Separate identities, constrain handlers and request filtering, protect configuration files, and review inherited policy. Monitor IIS logs, failed-request tracing in controlled diagnostics, and configuration changes.
IIS.gotcha: An IIS authentication setting does not automatically enforce application object ownership. Diagnose effective configuration rather than only the nearest web.config file.

MySQL.model: MySQL executes SQL under a database account whose grants, transaction state, and storage-engine behavior constrain application data access.
concepts: Design tables, keys, and indexes around invariants and access patterns. Transactions group changes; isolation and locking affect concurrent behavior.
Prepared statements bind values separately from SQL structure. Database, table, and column identifiers need explicit allowlists rather than value placeholders.
Accounts include host-matching rules and privileges. File, administrative, and network capabilities should not belong to ordinary application accounts.
MySQL.exercise: Create a disposable database and limited app account. Implement a parameterized insert/read and a rollback test; prove the app account cannot create users or access unrelated schemas.
MySQL.quick: Bind values; allowlist identifiers; use explicit transactions and least-privilege grants. Inspect query plans before adding indexes blindly.
MySQL.risk: String-built SQL and excessive database privileges can turn a query defect into broad data or host access.
MySQL.test: Submit an apostrophe-containing marker through a bound query and verify literal storage. Attempt an administrative operation with the app account and require denial.
MySQL.defense: Use prepared statements, minimal grants, encrypted connections, and protected backups. Monitor failed logins, unusual query shapes, privilege changes, and unexpected file-related operations.
MySQL.gotcha: Escaping depends on encoding and SQL mode; binding is preferable. Transaction guarantees depend on the storage engine and operation.

PostgreSQL.model: PostgreSQL organizes data into databases and schemas, with roles, privileges, MVCC transactions, and optional row-level security governing access.
concepts: Roles can own objects, inherit permissions, or assume other roles. Ownership and superuser-like capabilities exceed ordinary table privileges.
Use bound values and explicit schema qualification where trust matters. search_path influences object resolution, especially in privileged functions.
MVCC permits concurrent snapshots; isolation levels and constraints still determine correctness. Extensions and SECURITY DEFINER functions add privileged code paths.
PostgreSQL.exercise: Build a small transactional table under a nonowner app role. Test rollback, uniqueness, and tenant filtering; inspect a query plan and verify unrelated-schema denial.
PostgreSQL.quick: Parameterize values; secure search_path; separate migration ownership from runtime access. Test row-level policies using the actual runtime role.
PostgreSQL.risk: Unsafe SQL, writable schemas in trusted resolution paths, and misconfigured privileged functions or RLS can expose other tenants' data.
PostgreSQL.test: With two synthetic tenants, query both direct and joined paths under the app role and verify isolation. Confirm that an untrusted schema cannot shadow an object used by privileged code.
PostgreSQL.defense: Constrain grants and search paths, review SECURITY DEFINER functions, bind queries, and test RLS bypass conditions. Audit role changes, privileged functions, and unusual cross-tenant access.
PostgreSQL.gotcha: Table owners and BYPASSRLS roles can bypass ordinary row-level policy behavior; testing only as an administrator gives misleading results.

Web SQL Server.model: A web application reaches SQL Server through a driver and a database identity; query construction and that identity's permissions define the data boundary.
concepts: T-SQL expresses queries and transactions; indexes and execution plans shape performance. Logins authenticate at the server, while users and roles govern database access.
Use driver parameters with explicit types and lengths. Dynamic SQL inside stored procedures still needs safe binding and allowlisted structure.
Connection pooling reuses sessions; transaction and session state must not leak between requests. Encryption and certificate validation protect the client/server channel.
Web SQL Server.exercise: Create a limited database user and parameterized CRUD operation for synthetic notes. Test rollback, a quote-containing value, and denied access to another database.
Web SQL Server.quick: Prefer parameters over concatenation; separate migration and runtime identities; enforce TLS validation. See Windows SQL Server for enterprise service and linked-server concerns.
Web SQL Server.risk: Injection, overprivileged application logins, and unsafe dynamic stored procedures can expose data beyond the intended query.
Web SQL Server.test: Submit a harmless SQL-looking string as a value and verify literal handling. Confirm the runtime identity cannot alter logins, configuration, or unrelated tables.
Web SQL Server.defense: Bind typed parameters, minimize grants, review dynamic SQL, and encrypt connections. Correlate application request IDs with database auditing and suspicious permission changes.
Web SQL Server.gotcha: A stored procedure is not automatically injection-safe. Parameter placeholders cannot stand in for arbitrary table names or sort expressions.

SQLite.model: SQLite embeds a database engine in the application process and stores data in local files; operating-system file access is a primary security boundary.
concepts: Connections execute SQL against database files; journals/WAL and locking affect concurrency and durability.
Prepared statements bind values, while schema and SQL structure remain application code. Transactions should encompass related changes.
Extensions, attached databases, temporary files, and backup copies add access surfaces. There is no separate server account system equivalent to a network database.
SQLite.exercise: Create a temporary database, perform a transaction with rollback, and query a quote-containing value using parameters. Inspect file permissions and test a second writer's behavior.
SQLite.quick: Use bound parameters and explicit transactions. Protect the database, WAL/journal, and backup files together; disable unnecessary extension loading.
SQLite.risk: Unsafe SQL or readable database artifacts can expose application data even when no network database listener exists.
SQLite.test: Run the app under a restricted local identity and verify it cannot open an unrelated database file. Confirm malformed values remain data in a prepared query.
SQLite.defense: Use least-privilege filesystem access, parameterization, bounded inputs, and safe backup handling. Monitor unexpected database copies, attachments, and extension use.
SQLite.gotcha: Deleting a row does not guarantee immediate removal of all recoverable bytes from every database artifact or backup.

ORMs.model: An ORM translates object operations into database queries and tracks persistence state; it does not remove the database's transaction or authorization model.
concepts: Mappings and relationships determine joins, loading, and updates. Lazy loading can create N+1 queries; inspect generated SQL and execution plans.
Migrations change schema under a privileged deployment identity. Runtime queries should use a narrower identity.
Raw SQL, dynamic ordering, bulk updates, and mass assignment are escape hatches around higher-level safeguards. Unit-of-work lifetime influences consistency.
ORMs.exercise: Implement a parent/child query and compare lazy loading with explicit projection. Capture query counts, then test rollback and an update limited to approved fields.
ORMs.quick: Inspect generated SQL, parameter binding, query count, and transaction boundaries. Project response fields explicitly and allowlist writable properties.
ORMs.risk: Raw-query concatenation, tenant-filter bypass, and mass assignment can defeat the apparent safety of object-oriented persistence.
ORMs.test: Send an unexpected synthetic role/owner field in an update and verify rejection. Compare ordinary and bulk/raw paths for the same tenant constraint.
ORMs.defense: Use explicit DTOs and policies, bind raw values, constrain dynamic identifiers, and test every query path. Monitor slow queries and unexpected broad updates.
ORMs.gotcha: ORM parameterization does not authorize rows. Global filters may be bypassable by privileged APIs or raw queries.

MongoDB.model: MongoDB stores documents and evaluates structured queries and aggregation pipelines; a client-supplied object can alter query operators if merged without validation.
concepts: Collections, indexes, and document schemas shape access and performance. Flexible storage does not eliminate the need for application schemas.
Query operators and aggregation stages are executable query structure, distinct from scalar values. Build filters from trusted code.
Authentication, roles, network exposure, and driver configuration protect the database service. Multi-document operations may need explicit transactions.
MongoDB.exercise: Create a collection with a schema validator and limited user. Query by a validated scalar field, add an index, and test malformed types and unauthorized collections.
MongoDB.quick: Construct query objects explicitly; do not merge arbitrary request JSON into filters. Validate both types and allowed operators.
MongoDB.risk: Operator injection and overbroad service privileges can bypass intended filters or expose entire collections.
MongoDB.test: Send an object where the API expects a username string and verify schema rejection before querying. Confirm the app user cannot read an unrelated collection.
MongoDB.defense: Use strict input schemas, server-side authorization, narrow roles, and restricted network access. Log rejected operator-shaped inputs and unexpected collection access.
MongoDB.gotcha: NoSQL does not mean no injection. Sanitizing a few character sequences is not a substitute for constructing a typed query.

Redis.model: Redis provides in-memory data structures with optional persistence and messaging features; applications choose the durability and consistency semantics they need.
concepts: Strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, and expirations support different access patterns. Key naming should isolate applications and tenants.
Persistence modes and replication affect recovery; pub/sub is not a durable queue. Atomic commands differ from multi-step read/modify/write workflows.
ACLs constrain users, commands, and key patterns. Network binding, TLS, and operational commands determine the service's administrative surface.
Redis.exercise: Store a synthetic session with an expiry, observe TTL changes, and test a restricted ACL user against allowed and denied key prefixes.
Redis.quick: Bound TTL and value sizes; use atomic operations or appropriate transactions/scripts for invariants. Keep administrative commands out of runtime roles.
Redis.risk: Exposed Redis, broad command rights, shared key namespaces, and unsafe session caching can disclose data or alter application state.
Redis.test: Attempt to read a different synthetic tenant's prefix and run a denied administrative command with the app ACL user; both should fail.
Redis.defense: Restrict listeners, use ACLs/TLS, isolate key namespaces, and secure persistence files. Monitor authentication failures, configuration changes, evictions, and unexpected key access.
Redis.gotcha: Cache expiry is not authorization. Redis pub/sub messages are not replayed to disconnected subscribers.

Elasticsearch.model: Elasticsearch indexes documents for distributed search; mappings and query DSL determine interpretation, while cluster and index privileges constrain access.
concepts: Mappings distinguish analyzed text, exact keywords, numbers, and dates. Indexes and aliases organize data and routing.
Queries and aggregations can have substantial cost; deep pagination and wildcard-heavy operations need limits.
Authentication, index privileges, TLS, and management endpoints protect the cluster. An application search filter is not equivalent to an enforced tenant boundary.
Elasticsearch.exercise: Index synthetic records with explicit mappings and query them using a restricted role. Compare text and keyword behavior and enforce a bounded page size.
Elasticsearch.quick: Define mappings, constrain query shapes, limit result sizes, and use narrow index privileges. Do not expose the cluster directly as an unfiltered public search API.
Elasticsearch.risk: Unauthenticated clusters, overbroad roles, arbitrary DSL submission, and expensive queries can disclose data or exhaust resources.
Elasticsearch.test: Use the app identity to query an unrelated index and submit an over-limit aggregation in a disposable cluster; require denial or controlled rejection.
Elasticsearch.defense: Enforce service authentication and index policies, proxy only approved operations, and budget query cost. Monitor rejected operations, slow queries, and role changes.
Elasticsearch.gotcha: An alias or application-side filter does not automatically provide robust tenant isolation. Search results may lag writes according to refresh behavior.

Object Storage.model: S3 and Azure Blob store objects addressed by keys inside buckets/containers; access is governed by identity, resource policy, and optionally delegated signed URLs.
concepts: Keys are object identifiers, not necessarily filesystem paths. Metadata, content type, versioning, and lifecycle rules affect serving and retention.
Identity policies, bucket/container policies, public-access controls, and encryption keys interact. A signed URL delegates a specific operation for a bounded time.
Upload, processing, and download are separate trust boundaries. An object safe to store may still be unsafe to render or parse.
Object Storage.exercise: Use a dedicated sandbox or emulator to upload a text object privately and issue a short-lived read URL. Verify anonymous access fails and expiry removes delegated access.
Object Storage.quick: Default private; scope signed URLs to object/action/time; separate uploads from application origins. Record versioning and cleanup costs before using a cloud sandbox.
Object Storage.risk: Public policies, excessive signed-URL scope, and unsafe content serving can disclose data or introduce script/parser attacks.
Object Storage.test: Try an anonymous read and a signed URL for a different synthetic object. Both must fail unless explicitly authorized; verify uploaded markup is not executed on the application origin.
Object Storage.defense: Use public-access blocks, least-privilege policies, short delegation lifetimes, and isolated download origins. Audit policy changes, unusual downloads, and object access logs where enabled.
Object Storage.gotcha: An unguessable object key is not authorization. Encryption at rest does not prevent an overly permissive storage policy from returning plaintext.

Message Queues.model: A broker decouples producers and consumers; delivery, acknowledgement, retries, and ordering rules determine how reliably application state changes occur.
concepts: At-least-once delivery implies duplicates; consumers need idempotency. Acknowledging before durable work can lose effects, while acknowledging after work can repeat them.
Dead-letter queues isolate repeated failures but require review and retention policy. Ordering is usually scoped and can interact with parallel consumers.
Broker identity and queue/topic permissions differ from message-level authorization and validation. Serialized payloads remain untrusted input.
Message Queues.exercise: Run a local broker with a producer and idempotent consumer. Force a consumer restart after processing but before acknowledgement and show the duplicate does not repeat the business effect.
Message Queues.quick: Define delivery semantics, idempotency key, retry budget, dead-letter handling, and schema version. Separate producer, consumer, and administrator permissions.
Message Queues.risk: Unvalidated messages, overly broad broker roles, poison-message loops, and duplicate processing can alter state or exhaust capacity.
Message Queues.test: Publish a malformed synthetic message and verify bounded retries followed by quarantine. Confirm a producer identity cannot consume an unrelated queue.
Message Queues.defense: Validate schemas and message authority, enforce broker ACLs, implement idempotency, and cap retries. Monitor lag, redelivery, dead letters, and rejected identities.
Message Queues.gotcha: Exactly-once claims are usually scoped to a broker or transaction boundary, not every external side effect.

Sessions and Cookies.model: A session binds repeated requests to server-recognized state; cookies are a browser transport/storage mechanism that may carry a session identifier or signed state.
concepts: Use unpredictable identifiers, rotate after authentication/privilege changes, and enforce idle and absolute expiration. Logout must invalidate the server-side authority where applicable.
Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, Domain, and Path constrain different behavior. Host-only cookies reduce unnecessary subdomain scope.
Cookie credentials are ambient: the browser may attach them automatically. CSRF defenses and session theft defenses solve different problems.
Sessions and Cookies.exercise: Implement a synthetic login/logout flow and observe cookie attributes and identifier rotation. Verify the old identifier fails after logout and after privilege elevation.
Sessions and Cookies.quick: Use Secure and HttpOnly, an appropriate SameSite policy, narrow scope, and server-side expiry. Prefer __Host- cookie naming when its requirements fit.
Sessions and Cookies.risk: Session fixation, stolen tokens, weak invalidation, and missing CSRF protection let a valid session be used outside its intended workflow.
Sessions and Cookies.test: Set a prelogin synthetic identifier and confirm login rotates it. Replay the old session after logout and require rejection.
Sessions and Cookies.defense: Rotate and revoke session authority, protect cookies, validate CSRF tokens/origins as appropriate, and rate-limit sensitive flows. Monitor session reuse anomalies and authentication-state changes without logging identifiers.
Sessions and Cookies.gotcha: Cookie Path is not a strong isolation boundary. HttpOnly blocks script reads, not authenticated requests made by injected script.

Password Storage.model: Password verification compares a candidate against a deliberately expensive salted password hash; it should not require recovering the original password.
concepts: Use a maintained password-hashing library with Argon2id where supported; select work factors by current guidance and measured service capacity.
Unique salts prevent identical passwords from sharing stored hashes. Optional peppers require separate secret management and a rotation/recovery plan.
Login rate limiting, breach checks, reset tokens, and hash upgrades are separate lifecycle controls. Rehash after successful verification when policy changes.
Password Storage.exercise: Hash the same synthetic password twice and confirm different stored encodings both verify. Increase the configured cost and test upgrade-on-login without logging the password.
Password Storage.quick: Use library hash/verify APIs; never fast hashes alone or reversible encryption for ordinary password verification. Store algorithm and cost metadata with the hash.
Password Storage.risk: Fast or unsalted hashes, exposed reset tokens, weak recovery, and unlimited online attempts can defeat otherwise correct authentication.
Password Storage.test: Verify wrong passwords fail consistently and reset tokens are single-use and expire. Use only synthetic credentials and a small bounded test set.
Password Storage.defense: Apply modern hashing, rate limits, generic user-facing failures, protected resets, and MFA where appropriate. Monitor login/reset abuse while avoiding plaintext credentials in logs.
Password Storage.gotcha: A strong hash does not prevent online guessing or phishing. Do not silently truncate passwords without understanding library and policy behavior.

JWT.model: JWT packages claims inside a JOSE representation; accepting a token requires verifying its cryptography and the meaning of its claims for this application.
concepts: JWS provides integrity/authenticity, while JWE provides encryption. Base64url encoding is not secrecy.
Allowlist algorithms and trusted keys, then validate issuer, audience, time claims, token purpose, and application authorization.
Key discovery/rotation, token lifetime, refresh sessions, and revocation are operational policy. kid selects among trusted keys; it must not grant arbitrary file or network access.
JWT.exercise: Issue short-lived tokens from a local test issuer and verify them in a separate API. Test wrong audience, expired time, changed signature, and unsupported algorithm.
JWT.quick: Decode for inspection; verify before trust. Validate iss, aud, exp/nbf as applicable and distinguish access tokens from ID tokens.
JWT.risk: Signature bypass, algorithm/key confusion, and missing claim checks allow a token valid somewhere else or for another purpose to be accepted here.
JWT.test: Present a correctly signed token for a different synthetic audience and require rejection. Modify one claim without resigning and confirm verification fails.
JWT.defense: Use maintained JOSE libraries, fixed validation policy, trusted key sources, short lifetimes, and an explicit revocation model. Monitor token validation failures without storing raw tokens.
JWT.gotcha: A valid signature does not authorize every resource. A JWT payload is normally readable by whoever possesses the token.

OAuth2.model: OAuth delegates limited access from a resource owner through an authorization server to a client; it is not by itself a user-login identity protocol.
concepts: Authorization code with PKCE binds the code exchange to the initiating client instance. Distinguish public and confidential clients.
Exact redirect validation, state/correlation, requested scopes, and token audience constrain the flow. Do not put secrets in browser clients.
Access and refresh tokens have different lifetimes and storage requirements. Sender constraints, refresh rotation, and revocation depend on provider capabilities.
OAuth2.exercise: Connect a local client to a test authorization server using code plus PKCE. Record authorization, callback, token exchange, and API access with synthetic users.
OAuth2.quick: Use maintained protocol libraries, code+PKCE, exact redirects, bounded scopes, and correlation checks. Use OIDC when authenticated user identity is required.
OAuth2.risk: Redirect mistakes, missing correlation/PKCE, token leakage, and unsafe account linking can bind access to the wrong client or user.
OAuth2.test: Alter state and use the wrong PKCE verifier in the local flow; both must fail. Verify a token for another API is rejected by the resource server.
OAuth2.defense: Follow current OAuth security guidance, validate all endpoints and redirects, minimize scopes, and protect refresh tokens. Log correlation failures and suspicious grants without tokens.
OAuth2.gotcha: A client secret embedded in a mobile or browser app is not confidential. OAuth access tokens need not be JWTs.

OpenID Connect.model: OIDC adds authenticated identity claims and standardized discovery to OAuth, allowing a relying party to establish who authenticated at an issuer.
concepts: An ID token is intended for the client; an access token is intended for a resource server. Do not interchange them.
Validate issuer, audience, signature, time claims, and nonce where used; bind the response to the initiating browser session.
Discovery and JWKS supply metadata under a trusted issuer policy. UserInfo and account-linking identifiers must remain bound to the expected subject and issuer.
OpenID Connect.exercise: Use a test OIDC provider and local relying party. Inspect the verified issuer/subject pair, then test wrong audience and nonce mismatch.
OpenID Connect.quick: Identify accounts by stable issuer plus subject, not mutable email alone. Keep discovery tied to trusted issuers and use a maintained OIDC client.
OpenID Connect.risk: Issuer mix-up, ID/access-token confusion, nonce/correlation gaps, and email-only account linking can create incorrect login sessions.
OpenID Connect.test: Present a valid ID token from a second test issuer or client and require rejection. Confirm account linking requires a verified existing session and explicit policy.
OpenID Connect.defense: Pin trusted issuers, validate full token context, constrain redirects, and protect local sessions. Monitor issuer/audience/nonce failures and account-link changes.
OpenID Connect.gotcha: An email claim may be unverified or mutable. Successful OAuth authorization is not automatically a verified OIDC login.

SAML.model: SAML exchanges signed XML assertions between an identity provider and a service provider under configured metadata and trust relationships.
concepts: Assertions describe a subject, authentication, attributes, conditions, and audience; bindings transport protocol messages through browser or back-channel flows.
Verify the correct signed element and consume exactly the validated assertion. Audience, recipient, destination, time, and request correlation constrain acceptance.
Metadata, signing certificates, rollover, and identity mapping are operational trust decisions. XML parser configuration remains part of the security boundary.
SAML.exercise: Use a local test IdP/SP pair and inspect one synthetic login assertion. Test expired conditions, wrong audience, and an untrusted signing certificate.
SAML.quick: Use a maintained SAML library; validate signatures and protocol context together. Do not hand-roll XML signature verification or trust arbitrary embedded certificates.
SAML.risk: Signature-wrapping errors, incomplete conditions, weak request correlation, and unsafe XML parsing can make a service consume an assertion it did not validly trust.
SAML.test: Modify a signed assertion's harmless attribute and require rejection. Replay an already consumed response where the deployment expects single-use correlation and verify its policy.
SAML.defense: Use hardened parser/library settings, trusted metadata, replay controls, strict audiences/recipients, and tested certificate rollover. Log validation failures without full sensitive assertions.
SAML.gotcha: A signature somewhere in an XML document does not prove the exact data the application consumes is signed.

MFA and WebAuthn.model: MFA combines independent authentication factors; WebAuthn uses origin-bound public-key credentials to prove control of an authenticator without sharing a reusable password.
concepts: TOTP proves access to a shared seed but can be phished in real time. Recovery and factor replacement can be weaker than the primary factor.
WebAuthn registration creates a credential for a relying-party ID; assertions answer fresh challenges with origin/RP-bound signatures and policy flags.
Passkeys may be device-bound or synchronized depending on the platform. User verification, credential lifecycle, and account recovery need explicit relying-party policy.
MFA and WebAuthn.exercise: Register a test passkey in a local HTTPS/localhost relying party and authenticate with a fresh challenge. Verify replay and wrong-origin attempts fail; document recovery behavior separately.
MFA and WebAuthn.quick: Validate challenge, origin, RP ID, signature, and required user verification. Treat recovery and new-factor enrollment as sensitive authenticated operations.
MFA and WebAuthn.risk: Weak recovery, missing challenge/origin validation, or step-up enforced only in the UI can bypass an otherwise strong factor.
MFA and WebAuthn.test: Replay an old synthetic assertion and call a step-up-protected operation without completing the factor. Require server-side rejection in both cases.
MFA and WebAuthn.defense: Use mature WebAuthn libraries, short single-use challenges, strong enrollment/recovery checks, and audit factor changes. Alert on recovery abuse and unusual new-authenticator registration.
MFA and WebAuthn.gotcha: Two knowledge secrets are not two independent factors. Signature counters vary across authenticators and should not be treated as a universal replay oracle.

Docker.model: A container packages a process and filesystem view while sharing the host kernel; images, runtime configuration, and host privileges jointly determine isolation.
concepts: Images are layered artifacts; containers add writable state. Volumes and bind mounts can expose host data outside the image.
Namespaces limit views and capabilities limit selected privileged operations. Rootless operation and user mapping reduce some risks but do not make arbitrary code harmless.
Published ports, networks, secrets, build contexts, and the Docker socket create distinct boundaries. Image provenance and runtime permissions must be reviewed separately.
Docker.exercise: Run a harmless web image bound to loopback with a read-only filesystem and minimal writable volume. Inspect its identity, mounts, capabilities, and network exposure, then remove it.
Docker.quick: Avoid privileged mode and Docker-socket mounts; pin image digests for reproducibility; keep build contexts small and secrets out of layers.
Docker.risk: Privileged containers, sensitive host mounts, exposed daemons, and leaked build secrets can turn container access into host or credential exposure.
Docker.test: Attempt to write outside the designated volume and access an unmounted host marker from the lab container. Both should fail; inspect the actual published host address.
Docker.defense: Use nonroot/rootless modes where compatible, drop capabilities, constrain mounts/networks, patch images and host kernels, and scan build artifacts. Monitor daemon access and unusual container privileges.
Docker.gotcha: Deleting a secret in a later image layer does not remove it from earlier layers. Container isolation is not equivalent to a separate kernel VM.

Kubernetes.model: Kubernetes reconciles declared workloads and infrastructure through API objects, controllers, and node agents; cluster identity and workload isolation are separate policy layers.
concepts: Pods run containers; Deployments manage replicas; Services provide stable discovery; Ingress implementations route external traffic.
RBAC controls API operations for users and service accounts. Secrets are objects requiring access and storage protection, not automatically safe merely because they are base64 encoded.
Admission policy, workload security settings, network policies, and node isolation constrain what workloads can do. NetworkPolicy enforcement depends on the network implementation.
Kubernetes.exercise: Use a disposable local cluster to deploy a nonroot app with resource limits and a dedicated service account. Test allowed API actions and a network policy between two toy workloads.
Kubernetes.quick: Minimize service-account tokens and RBAC; enforce restricted workload settings; set requests/limits; verify network policies actually work.
Kubernetes.risk: Overprivileged service accounts, privileged pods, exposed control planes, and unrestricted east-west access can expand a workload compromise across the cluster.
Kubernetes.test: From a test service account, attempt a forbidden secret read and require denial. Verify a blocked pod-to-pod connection fails with the chosen CNI.
Kubernetes.defense: Use least-privilege RBAC, admission controls, restricted pods, secret encryption, and network segmentation. Audit API requests, privilege changes, and unexpected pod specs.
Kubernetes.gotcha: Namespaces organize resources but are not complete security boundaries. A policy manifest has no effect unless its enforcing component supports it.

CI and CD.model: A CI/CD workflow executes repository-selected code with runner resources and automation credentials, then promotes artifacts across trust boundaries.
concepts: GitHub Actions events determine which code and context are trusted. Jobs, steps, reusable workflows, and environments have separate permission and approval choices.
GITHUB_TOKEN permissions should be explicit and minimal. OIDC federation can replace long-lived cloud secrets when claims and trust policies are constrained.
Actions, dependencies, caches, and uploaded artifacts are supply-chain inputs. Untrusted pull-request code must not inherit privileged deployment credentials.
CI and CD.exercise: Create a toy build workflow with read-only permissions and a separate manually approved deployment job. Verify forked/untrusted changes cannot access a synthetic protected value.
CI and CD.quick: Pin third-party actions to reviewed commits when practical; constrain events and permissions; separate build from deployment; bind OIDC trust to intended repository/ref/environment.
CI and CD.risk: Executing untrusted code in a privileged event, script interpolation, cache poisoning, or broad tokens can compromise releases and repositories.
CI and CD.test: Review a synthetic pull request path and verify no privileged job executes its code with secrets. Confirm unexpected OIDC subjects fail the sandbox trust policy.
CI and CD.defense: Use least-privilege tokens, protected environments, safe argument passing, trusted artifacts, and dependency review. Audit workflow edits, token use, and deployment provenance.
CI and CD.gotcha: pull_request_target can run in a privileged base-repository context; checking out untrusted head code there is a distinct risk. Masking logs is not secret isolation.

Reverse Proxies CDN and WAF.model: An intermediary terminates or forwards client traffic and may route, cache, or filter it; the origin must know which intermediary-provided facts it can trust.
concepts: Forwarded host, scheme, and client-address headers are trustworthy only from configured hops. Edge TLS does not automatically protect the origin connection.
CDNs distribute/cache content; WAFs apply request rules. Neither replaces application authorization or correct parsing.
Origin reachability, protocol translation, header normalization, cache keys, and timeouts shape the effective request path.
Reverse Proxies CDN and WAF.exercise: Place a local proxy before a toy app and record the method, authority, path, and client identity seen at each hop. Try direct-origin access and forged forwarding headers.
Reverse Proxies CDN and WAF.quick: Define trusted hops, canonical authority, origin access policy, and edge/origin timeouts. Compare parsing and caching decisions end to end.
Reverse Proxies CDN and WAF.risk: Origin bypass, spoofed forwarding headers, parsing disagreement, and overconfidence in WAF rules can defeat edge controls.
Reverse Proxies CDN and WAF.test: Reach the lab origin directly and verify its network/authentication policy blocks bypass. Send a fake forwarded scheme from an untrusted client and confirm it is not accepted.
Reverse Proxies CDN and WAF.defense: Restrict origin access, authenticate trusted proxy paths, overwrite untrusted headers, and patch parsers. Correlate edge and origin logs and test rules with harmless markers.
Reverse Proxies CDN and WAF.gotcha: A WAF block is evidence about a specific request and rule, not proof that a vulnerability is fixed.

HTTP Caching.model: An HTTP cache reuses stored responses when the cache key, freshness, validation, and policy permit it; a shared cache can serve many different users.
concepts: Cache-Control controls freshness and reuse; validators such as ETag support conditional requests. no-cache requires revalidation, while no-store forbids storage by compliant caches.
Vary selects request headers that distinguish representations. Cache keys may also depend on CDN/proxy configuration beyond standard URL components.
Authentication, cookies, redirects, errors, and personalized content require deliberate shared-cache policy. Edge and application views of paths must agree.
HTTP Caching.exercise: Serve a public versioned response with an ETag and a private user response. Observe fresh hits, revalidation, and account switching through a local shared cache.
HTTP Caching.quick: Separate public immutable assets from personalized responses. Document key inputs, TTL, Vary, purge behavior, and no-store decisions.
HTTP Caching.risk: Unkeyed attacker input can poison a shared response; path/policy confusion can cache one user's private response for another.
HTTP Caching.test: Vary a harmless request header that changes the origin response and verify it is either keyed or never shared. Check that two synthetic users never receive each other's private content.
HTTP Caching.defense: Align cache keys with response variation, restrict cacheability, canonicalize consistently, and test authenticated paths. Monitor hit/miss headers and anomalous cross-user response markers.
HTTP Caching.gotcha: Cache-Control: no-cache does not mean do not store. A browser-only test can miss shared CDN behavior.

AWS.model: AWS resources live within accounts and regions, while IAM and resource policies determine which principals can perform which actions under specified conditions.
concepts: Prefer roles and temporary STS credentials over long-lived keys. Identity, resource, organization, session, and boundary policies can interact.
VPC routing, security groups, endpoints, and public addressing govern reachability; IAM still governs service API authority.
Compute metadata, storage policies, logging, encryption keys, and deployment identities are separate attack surfaces. Sandbox budgets and teardown are part of lab design.
AWS.exercise: In a dedicated budgeted sandbox, create a role limited to one synthetic storage resource and verify allowed/denied actions. Enable relevant logging and delete resources after the exercise.
AWS.quick: Use temporary roles, narrow actions/resources/conditions, explicit public-access controls, and budgets. Never experiment in an employer or production account.
AWS.risk: Overbroad IAM, public resources, exposed credentials, and metadata reachable through vulnerable applications can expand an application flaw into cloud access.
AWS.test: Use the sandbox role against an unapproved resource and require denial. Review the workload's metadata protection and permissions without retrieving real production credentials.
AWS.defense: Apply least privilege, protect metadata access, block unintended public exposure, and collect CloudTrail/service logs. Alert on privilege changes, unusual role assumptions, and disabled logging.
AWS.gotcha: A private subnet does not imply minimal IAM privileges. Budgets alert on cost; they are not always hard spending caps.

Azure.model: Azure separates tenant identity, subscription/resource organization, management-plane permissions, and service data-plane access.
concepts: Entra principals and managed identities receive RBAC assignments at scopes. Management and data roles can grant different authority.
Virtual networks, private endpoints, firewalls, and public service endpoints determine reachability independently of identity checks.
Managed identity tokens, Key Vault, storage policies, resource logs, and deployment permissions require explicit lifecycle and monitoring choices.
Azure.exercise: Use a dedicated sandbox subscription to give a managed identity access to one synthetic resource. Test a denied second resource, inspect activity logs, and tear down all lab resources.
Azure.quick: Prefer managed identities, minimal scoped roles, private access where appropriate, and monitored budgets. Distinguish tenant administration from subscription/resource administration.
Azure.risk: Overbroad role assignments, exposed storage, leaked application credentials, and unprotected workload metadata can expose cloud resources.
Azure.test: Attempt an unapproved data-plane action with the lab identity and require denial. Verify that a management role does not accidentally imply the data access your design intended to withhold.
Azure.defense: Review role scopes, protect identity endpoints, restrict public access, and audit managed-identity use. Monitor role assignments, secret access, and logging changes.
Azure.gotcha: An Azure resource's network restriction and its RBAC policy are separate controls. Cost alerts do not replace teardown.

Serverless.model: A serverless function runs provider-managed compute in response to events, with an execution identity and lifecycle that may be reused across invocations.
concepts: HTTP, queue, storage, and scheduled triggers have different authentication, retry, and ordering semantics.
Execution identity and environment/configuration determine reachable services. Least privilege must fit each function's actual task.
Warm-instance state, concurrency, time limits, and deployment packaging affect correctness. Event input and upstream service metadata remain untrusted.
Serverless.exercise: Deploy a small function in a dedicated sandbox with a narrow role and a synthetic event. Test invalid input, retry behavior, and cleanup of temporary state.
Serverless.quick: Validate events, bound work, make retried operations idempotent, and minimize the execution role. Keep secrets out of packages and logs.
Serverless.risk: Overprivileged identities, unvalidated events, dependency compromise, and cross-invocation state assumptions can expose data or repeat harmful side effects.
Serverless.test: Replay the same synthetic event and verify one business effect. Attempt access to an unrelated resource with the function identity and require denial.
Serverless.defense: Use least-privilege roles, schema validation, idempotency keys, concurrency limits, and safe secret retrieval. Monitor invocations, retries, denied actions, and abnormal duration/cost.
Serverless.gotcha: Serverless does not mean stateless by guarantee or responsibility-free security. Provider isolation does not validate application events.

Terraform.model: Terraform compares desired resource configuration with provider-reported state and plans operations; its state and execution identity are sensitive infrastructure control surfaces.
concepts: Providers implement APIs; resources and modules express dependencies. Plans are previews tied to particular configuration, state, and environment.
State records resource attributes and can contain secrets despite sensitive output annotations. Remote backends need access controls, encryption, and locking.
Provider/module supply chains, execution credentials, drift, and destructive plans require review. Separate planning and applying privileges where practical.
Terraform.exercise: Use a disposable local or budgeted cloud resource, inspect a plan, apply it, introduce harmless drift, and plan again. Verify state access and destroy only the lab resource.
Terraform.quick: Review plan changes, pin providers/modules, protect state, and use scoped short-lived credentials. Never assume sensitive annotations remove values from state.
Terraform.risk: Leaked state, malicious providers/modules, broad apply credentials, and unreviewed destructive changes can compromise infrastructure.
Terraform.test: Place a dummy secret in a lab resource and inspect where it appears in state versus console output. Verify an unauthorized identity cannot read the backend.
Terraform.defense: Secure and version state, require reviewed plans, constrain credentials, and validate provider provenance. Audit backend access and unexpected resource or IAM changes.
Terraform.gotcha: A previously approved plan may no longer match current intent or drift. Removing a resource from configuration can schedule destruction.

Recon and Subdomain Enumeration.model: Recon builds an evidence-backed asset inventory within written authorization; discovered names are hypotheses, not automatic permission to test.
concepts: Separate passive sources such as certificate transparency from active DNS/HTTP checks. Record source, timestamp, ownership confidence, and scope status.
Wildcard DNS, shared hosting, stale records, and third-party services can create misleading matches. Validate resolution and service identity before testing.
Rate limits, exclusion lists, and stop conditions apply throughout collection. Keep corporate/private target data out of public notes.
Recon and Subdomain Enumeration.exercise: Inventory only a domain you control or an explicit training target using passive records and a small approved active check. Mark unresolved and third-party assets rather than silently treating them as in scope.
Recon and Subdomain Enumeration.quick: Track asset, evidence, owner, scope, resolver result, service identity, and next hypothesis. Discovery is not exploitation authorization.
Recon and Subdomain Enumeration.risk: Unbounded enumeration or ownership assumptions can touch unrelated services, violate program rules, and produce false findings.
Recon and Subdomain Enumeration.test: Include a known wildcard and a third-party CNAME in a local test zone; verify the inventory flags both for review instead of treating them as unique owned hosts.
Recon and Subdomain Enumeration.defense: Maintain exclusions and request budgets, validate ownership, and retain reproducible evidence. Stop on unexpected data exposure or out-of-scope routing.
Recon and Subdomain Enumeration.gotcha: A certificate name can be historical or shared. A dangling DNS record is not proof that the referenced service is currently claimable.

Content Discovery.model: Content discovery maps reachable routes and resources using observed application behavior and bounded hypotheses about unlinked content.
concepts: Start from navigation, scripts, API schemas, and observed requests before dictionary probing. Track authenticated and unauthenticated views separately.
Establish baselines for missing paths, redirects, soft 404s, wildcard routes, and response-size variation.
Method, host, content type, session, and parameters can change routing. Request volume and destructive endpoints require explicit controls.
Content Discovery.exercise: Map a local vulnerable app by crawling and a small curated wordlist. Compare responses with randomized nonexistent paths and record only reproducible distinctions.
Content Discovery.quick: Baseline first; bound concurrency and rate; retain method/status/length/redirect/context. Do not infer validity from status code alone.
Content Discovery.risk: Aggressive probing can trigger expensive operations, create data, or cross scope; soft 404s can inflate false positives.
Content Discovery.test: Add a catch-all route to a toy app and verify the discovery process filters it using content and baseline comparison rather than 200 status alone.
Content Discovery.defense: Use read-only probes where possible, explicit exclusions, and stop conditions. For defenders, monitor abnormal path diversity and constrain expensive unauthenticated routes.
Content Discovery.gotcha: Different response length can reflect a nonce or timestamp rather than a real endpoint. Authentication state must be stable during comparisons.

Burp Workflow.model: A proxy workflow turns browser actions into reproducible request hypotheses, controlled modifications, and evidence; tool mechanics live in the shared Burp Suite note.
concepts: Define project scope and a dedicated browser profile before interception. Keep unrelated browsing and credentials out of the project.
Use history to establish a baseline, Repeater for one-variable tests, and comparisons to distinguish genuine effects from session or nonce changes.
Session renewal, CSRF tokens, redirects, and caching can invalidate comparisons. Record the exact identity and prerequisite state for every finding.
Burp Workflow.exercise: Capture a local app action, replay it unchanged, then change one harmless parameter. Save baseline, test, and response evidence with synthetic identities and a concise hypothesis.
Burp Workflow.quick: Scope -> baseline -> one-variable change -> compare -> reproduce -> document -> clean up. Link [[Burp Suite]] for tool-specific operations.
Burp Workflow.risk: Out-of-scope interception, stale sessions, and uncontrolled automated requests can expose data or produce misleading results.
Burp Workflow.test: Send a request after deliberate logout and verify the workflow detects the changed session instead of attributing the response to the modified parameter.
Burp Workflow.defense: Use scope filters, request limits, synthetic accounts, and redacted evidence. Keep interception CA trust confined to the lab profile and remove it when retired.
Burp Workflow.gotcha: A replayed request may not reproduce a browser action when anti-CSRF state, timing, or redirects matter. Scanner availability varies by edition.

Source Code Review.model: Security review follows untrusted inputs through transformations to sensitive operations while checking authorization and invariants at each boundary.
concepts: Map entry points, identity establishment, data models, and dangerous sinks. Prefer a concrete call path over an indiscriminate keyword list.
Review configuration, dependencies, serialization, error paths, and background jobs alongside request handlers.
A suspicious API is a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability. Reproduce the relevant condition in an isolated test and identify the owning validation boundary.
Source Code Review.exercise: Trace one local endpoint from request parsing to database write and response. Write a focused negative test for ownership and one for malformed input, then document the controlling checks.
Source Code Review.quick: Record source -> transformations -> policy -> sink, including identity and version assumptions. Verify fixes with the smallest failing behavior test.
Source Code Review.risk: Missing indirect call paths, trusting annotations without runtime tests, or ignoring deployment configuration can leave exploitable gaps.
Source Code Review.test: Introduce a harmless ownership-check omission in a disposable sample and confirm the negative test fails; restore the check and require the same test to pass.
Source Code Review.defense: Use threat-focused review checklists, structured input/output models, centralized policies, and regression tests. Keep findings evidence-based and distinguish reachable defects from theoretical patterns.
Source Code Review.gotcha: A grep hit alone is not impact. Generated code and framework middleware can change the actual control path.

Bug Bounty Methodology.model: A bounty assessment is constrained research under a program's authorization and disclosure rules, with minimal-impact validation and reproducible reporting.
concepts: Read scope, prohibited tests, data-handling rules, rate limits, and safe-harbor terms before requests. Recheck scope when redirects or third-party services appear.
Prioritize hypotheses from architecture and observed behavior; validate with synthetic accounts and the least data needed to demonstrate impact.
Track duplicates, prerequisites, severity rationale, evidence, disclosure timing, and retest status. A possible weakness is not automatically a bounty-eligible finding.
Bug Bounty Methodology.exercise: Perform a mock assessment of a local vulnerable app under a written scope. Produce one reproducible report with two synthetic accounts and no unrelated data access.
Bug Bounty Methodology.quick: Scope first; minimize impact; stop on unexpected sensitive data; report promptly; retest only within authorization.
Bug Bounty Methodology.risk: Testing outside scope, unnecessary data collection, persistence, or availability impact can harm third parties and violate authorization.
Bug Bounty Methodology.test: Add an out-of-scope redirect to the mock target and verify the workflow stops instead of following it into active testing.
Bug Bounty Methodology.defense: Use explicit boundaries, bounded requests, evidence redaction, and documented stop conditions. Keep private program information out of public writeups until permitted.
Bug Bounty Methodology.gotcha: Publicly reachable does not mean authorized. A program's acceptance criteria and legal authorization are related but distinct concerns.

Reporting.model: A useful report connects reproducible evidence to a security boundary, concrete impact, and a fix that can be independently retested.
concepts: State target/version, prerequisites, identities, exact steps, expected behavior, observed behavior, and minimal evidence.
Explain impact without inflating it; separate demonstrated effects from plausible but untested extensions. Include severity assumptions and affected scope.
Remediation should address the controlling cause and include a regression test. Redact secrets and comply with platform writeup rules.
Reporting.exercise: Write a report for a local ownership-check defect using two synthetic users. Ask whether another reader can reproduce it without guessing state, then add a retest proving the fix.
Reporting.quick: Summary -> prerequisites -> steps -> evidence -> impact -> root cause -> fix -> retest. Label unknowns and avoid unsupported execution claims.
Reporting.risk: Missing prerequisites, excessive sensitive evidence, or speculative impact can make a report unsafe or impossible to triage.
Reporting.test: Give only the report to a fresh lab session and verify the documented steps reproduce the same result. Confirm redacted artifacts retain enough context without exposing credentials.
Reporting.defense: Use synthetic data, stable request IDs, explicit versions, and bounded proof. Keep customer-facing findings concise and technical evidence in a controlled attachment.
Reporting.gotcha: Screenshots alone often omit request details and identity context. A fixed UI is not a successful retest if the underlying endpoint remains vulnerable.

XSS.model: XSS occurs when attacker-controlled data reaches a browser execution context without the required separation, encoding, or sanitization.
concepts: Reflected input returns in the current response; stored input reaches later readers; DOM-based XSS follows client-side source-to-sink flow. These categories can overlap.
HTML text, attributes, JavaScript, CSS, and URLs require different handling. Blind execution refers to an observation gap, not a different root cause.
Trace query, fragment, storage, and message sources into innerHTML, document.write, or other dangerous sinks; confirm actual execution rather than mere reflection.
XSS.exercise: Complete the Academy's introductory reflected and stored XSS labs, then replace one unsafe sink in a local toy page with textContent. Record the execution context and the corrected behavior.
XSS.quick: In a deliberately vulnerable HTML lab, use a harmless marker such as ``; do not collect cookies or contact external endpoints. Adapt tests to the actual context, not a universal payload list.
XSS.risk: The attacker needs a controllable source and a reachable executable sink; execution gains the affected origin's browser privileges, subject to browser controls.
XSS.test: Insert the marker into the isolated vulnerable sink, observe only the local alert, then verify literal/sanitized rendering after the fix.
XSS.defense: Use safe DOM APIs and contextual encoding; sanitize supported rich HTML with a maintained library. Add restrictive CSP and Trusted Types where supported, plus regression tests for every sink.
XSS.gotcha: Blacklist removal of one tag or event is fragile; parser context and alternate sinks matter. CSP is defense in depth, and HttpOnly does not prevent script from acting through the user's session.

CSRF.model: CSRF abuses automatically attached credentials to cause an unwanted state-changing request without proving the user's intent.
concepts: Cookie-authenticated form actions are common targets; login CSRF and token/session binding failures are separate variants.
A request may be sent even when SOP prevents reading the response. SameSite is a site-based control, not a complete origin or intent check.
Find state-changing routes and inspect token generation, validation, method handling, Origin/Referer policy, and cookie behavior.
CSRF.exercise: Use a local two-origin form demo or an Academy CSRF lab. Change only a synthetic profile value, then add a session-bound token and repeat.
CSRF.quick: Compare a valid request with missing, wrong, and another session's token. Check state on the server; a browser CORS error alone does not prove the action was blocked.
CSRF.risk: The victim must carry usable ambient credentials and the endpoint must accept an attacker-inducible request without an effective intent check.
CSRF.test: Submit the local state-changing form from a second origin and verify the protected version rejects it without a valid token.
CSRF.defense: Use maintained CSRF middleware, session-bound tokens, appropriate SameSite cookies, and origin checks. Keep GET safe and protect login and sensitive account changes.
CSRF.gotcha: Checking a token only when present, accepting another session's token, or relying solely on a same-site sibling boundary can undermine protection.

Clickjacking.model: Clickjacking overlays or disguises a framed trusted interface so a user activates a control under a false visual context.
concepts: Basic framing, multi-step interactions, and drag/drop UI redress differ in user interaction and feasibility.
The target must be frameable and the relevant authenticated state/control must function inside the frame.
Inspect frame-ancestors and X-Frame-Options, then verify actual browser behavior rather than relying only on header presence.
Clickjacking.exercise: Frame a harmless local preference page and attempt one visible test interaction. Add frame-ancestors and confirm the browser refuses the embedding.
Clickjacking.quick: Use a transparent/positioned frame only in a toy page with a harmless action. Document required clicks, session state, and browser framing behavior.
Clickjacking.risk: Impact depends on a meaningful available action and a plausible interaction; simply framing a public page is not automatically a security finding.
Clickjacking.test: Load the protected local page from an unapproved parent origin and verify no interactive frame is available.
Clickjacking.defense: Use CSP frame-ancestors with an explicit embedding policy, retain appropriate legacy X-Frame-Options if needed, and require deliberate confirmation for sensitive actions.
Clickjacking.gotcha: Frame-busting JavaScript is weaker than enforced framing policy. frame-ancestors must be delivered as an HTTP response policy, not a meta-only substitute.

CORS Misconfiguration.model: A CORS misconfiguration grants an unintended origin permission to read a response through browser script, potentially with ambient credentials.
concepts: Arbitrary origin reflection, weak allowlist matching, trusted null origins, and compromised trusted origins have different prerequisites.
Credentialed reads require an explicit allowed origin and credential permission; a wildcard origin is not a valid credentialed-read grant.
Inspect simple and preflighted requests, credential mode, Vary: Origin, and whether the response actually contains sensitive data.
CORS Misconfiguration.exercise: Use two local origins and synthetic session data. Compare a denied origin with a deliberately reflected one, then replace reflection with an exact allowlist.
CORS Misconfiguration.quick: Record Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Credentials, and the browser-readable result. Test in a browser, not only with curl.
CORS Misconfiguration.risk: A harmful case requires an unintended readable response and useful victim authority or data; permissive access to intentionally public content may be harmless.
CORS Misconfiguration.test: From an unapproved lab origin, attempt a credentialed fetch and confirm JavaScript cannot read the protected response.
CORS Misconfiguration.defense: Use exact trusted-origin policies, least-needed methods/headers, appropriate cache variation, and independent authentication/authorization. Avoid trusting null by default.
CORS Misconfiguration.gotcha: Substring or suffix checks can trust unintended hosts. CORS does not stop nonbrowser clients and is not a CSRF defense by itself.

SQL Injection.model: SQL injection occurs when untrusted data changes a query's syntax instead of remaining a bound value.
concepts: In-band results/errors and blind boolean/time observations are different evidence channels. Database dialect and driver behavior determine valid syntax.
Value contexts differ from identifiers, sort expressions, and raw stored-procedure SQL. Binding values does not safely parameterize arbitrary query structure.
Trace input to executed SQL and use controlled differential tests; errors alone can indicate validation failures rather than confirmed injection.
SQL Injection.exercise: Complete introductory Academy SQL injection labs or compare concatenated and parameterized queries over a local table of synthetic records.
SQL Injection.quick: Start with a harmless quote-containing marker, then use lab-provided boolean comparisons to demonstrate changed query logic. Avoid production data extraction or destructive statements.
SQL Injection.risk: Impact depends on the reachable query, returned data, and database account privileges; stacked statements and host access are not universal capabilities.
SQL Injection.test: Verify the fixed query stores/searches a SQL-looking string literally and returns only the authorized synthetic records.
SQL Injection.defense: Bind values, allowlist dynamic identifiers, minimize grants, and constrain error disclosure. Add regression tests at every raw-query boundary and monitor anomalous query failures.
SQL Injection.gotcha: Escaping can fail across encodings or modes. ORMs and stored procedures remain vulnerable when their escape hatches concatenate untrusted data.

NoSQL Injection.model: NoSQL injection lets attacker data become query operators, expressions, or structural fragments rather than validated values.
concepts: Operator injection changes structured query objects; syntax injection targets string-built expressions or evaluation features.
An object supplied where a string was expected can alter matching even without SQL-like punctuation.
Inspect request parsing, query construction, schema validation, and driver-specific operator handling.
NoSQL Injection.exercise: Use an Academy NoSQL lab or a local synthetic-user collection. Compare an explicitly constructed scalar filter with a filter built by merging request objects.
NoSQL Injection.quick: Test type confusion first: send an object/array where the API expects a scalar and inspect whether validation rejects it before database use.
NoSQL Injection.risk: A query-building path must accept attacker-controlled structure or expression syntax; the exact effect depends on the database and operation.
NoSQL Injection.test: Submit an operator-shaped object to the protected toy endpoint and require a schema error rather than broader record matching.
NoSQL Injection.defense: Construct queries from trusted code, validate types and fields, disallow unneeded operators, and minimize database roles. Log malformed query-shaped inputs without sensitive values.
NoSQL Injection.gotcha: Removing dollar signs alone does not cover all expression or type-confusion paths. Different NoSQL systems have different query languages.

Command Injection.model: Command injection occurs when untrusted input changes shell syntax or an executable's intended arguments.
concepts: Shell metacharacter injection differs from argument injection into a directly invoked program. Avoiding a shell removes one boundary, not all option parsing risks.
Visible output and bounded blind observations are different evidence paths; platform shell syntax varies.
Trace request values into process APIs, quoting layers, executable selection, and option construction.
Command Injection.exercise: Compare a deliberately vulnerable local shell wrapper with a fixed executable/argument-list implementation. Use only a marker-printing operation in the toy process.
Command Injection.quick: Prefer library APIs; otherwise use a fixed executable and structured arguments. Treat leading-dash values and tool-specific response/config-file syntax as separate concerns.
Command Injection.risk: The process runs under the application's OS identity, so impact depends on its privileges, environment, and reachable resources.
Command Injection.test: Pass a harmless semicolon-containing marker and verify the safe version passes one data argument without launching an additional command.
Command Injection.defense: Avoid shell construction, allowlist operations and arguments, use end-of-options separators where supported, and run with minimal privilege. Monitor unexpected child processes and command lines with appropriate redaction.
Command Injection.gotcha: Shell escaping is platform-specific. Direct execution can still be unsafe when attacker data selects dangerous program options.

Path Traversal.model: Path traversal lets a caller escape an intended resource root because path parsing, normalization, or filesystem resolution is not constrained correctly.
concepts: Relative dot segments, absolute paths, alternate separators, decoding differences, and archive entry paths are distinct variants.
Symlinks and reparse points can change the final filesystem target after textual normalization; race conditions can matter.
Inspect every decoding/joining step and compare the final resolved resource with the authorized root.
Path Traversal.exercise: Create a local served directory and a harmless marker file just outside it. Test a relative traversal in a toy endpoint, then enforce containment and repeat.
Path Traversal.quick: Use server-selected resource IDs where possible. If accepting paths, validate canonical containment with filesystem semantics, not a naive string prefix.
Path Traversal.risk: The service identity must be able to access the escaped resource; read, write, and archive-extraction paths have different consequences.
Path Traversal.test: Request `../outside-marker.txt` only against the disposable directory fixture and confirm the fixed endpoint cannot return it.
Path Traversal.defense: Constrain resolved paths, reject absolute/unsupported forms, use safe archive extraction, and minimize filesystem privileges. Log denied path variants and unexpected file access.
Path Traversal.gotcha: Replacing one ../ occurrence is insufficient. A path beginning with the same text as the allowed directory may still be a sibling, not a child.

File Upload Attacks.model: An upload crosses several boundaries: filename, stored bytes, processing pipeline, and later serving context. Safety must hold at each stage.
concepts: Extension/MIME mismatches, active content, parser vulnerabilities, archive paths, and oversized files represent different attack classes.
A file harmless to store may be dangerous to parse or serve inline on a trusted origin.
Inspect storage location, naming, execution handlers, processor privileges, download headers, and access control.
File Upload Attacks.exercise: Build a local text/image upload endpoint with server-generated names and isolated storage. Test a mismatched extension, oversized file, and harmless HTML marker served as an attachment.
File Upload Attacks.quick: Allowlist formats, verify actual content with maintained parsers, bound size, generate names, and separate upload serving from the application origin.
File Upload Attacks.risk: Impact requires a downstream interpretation or access-control mistake; acceptance of an unusual extension alone does not prove execution.
File Upload Attacks.test: Upload harmless markup and verify it cannot execute on the application origin or select an executable server handler.
File Upload Attacks.defense: Use nonexecuting storage, sandbox processors, validate formats, constrain archives, and authorize downloads. Monitor rejected formats, processing failures, and unexpected executable mappings.
File Upload Attacks.gotcha: Client Content-Type is untrusted. Antivirus scanning is one control, not a replacement for safe storage and serving architecture.

SSRF.model: SSRF lets untrusted input influence a server-originated request, borrowing the server's network position or service identity.
concepts: Direct fetches, redirects, URL parsers, DNS resolution changes, and non-HTTP schemes can create different request paths.
Blind cases reveal only an observable side effect, while in-band cases return fetched data. Restrict demonstrations to owned lab services.
Trace URL validation through redirects and final connection establishment; compare the validated host with the actual destination.
SSRF.exercise: Use two local toy services: a public fetcher and a private marker endpoint. Demonstrate the unsafe fetch only inside that isolated network, then enforce a narrow destination policy.
SSRF.quick: Allowlist schemes and destinations, resolve/check addresses deliberately, and revalidate redirects. Do not use real cloud metadata or corporate internal services as test targets.
SSRF.risk: Impact depends on server reachability, allowed methods/headers, returned data, and any attached credentials.
SSRF.test: Request the private lab marker through the fixed fetcher and require denial, including when an allowed toy URL redirects to it.
SSRF.defense: Use a constrained fetch service, egress filtering, safe URL parsing, redirect limits, and no ambient privileged credentials. Monitor unexpected outbound destinations and denied private-address requests.
SSRF.gotcha: A hostname allowlist checked before redirects or DNS changes can be insufficient. Blocking one textual loopback representation is not a complete address policy.

XXE.model: XXE arises when an XML parser resolves attacker-influenced external entities or related resources beyond the application's intended data boundary.
concepts: External general/parameter entities, DTD processing, and parser-specific resolution features vary by library and configuration.
In-band data and blind I/O observations are separate variants; entity expansion can also create availability risks.
Identify the actual XML parser and its DTD, external resolver, XInclude, and resource-limit settings.
XXE.exercise: Use a local parser fixture and a harmless local marker file. Compare permissive resolution with DTD/external-resource processing disabled; never target system secrets.
XXE.quick: Disable unneeded DTD/external resolution and use a rejecting resolver. Verify the library's current defaults instead of assuming every XML API behaves alike.
XXE.risk: A vulnerable parser may access files or network resources under its service identity; exposure depends on enabled features and permissions.
XXE.test: Parse the lab document with a marker reference and confirm no file or network resolution occurs in the protected configuration.
XXE.defense: Use hardened parser settings, bounded size/depth/expansion, narrow service permissions, and safe schemas. Monitor parser errors and unexpected parser-originated I/O.
XXE.gotcha: Disabling one entity option may not disable every external-resource feature. Safe defaults can change when wrappers or libraries override settings.

SSTI.model: SSTI occurs when user-controlled data becomes server-side template source and is evaluated as template logic.
concepts: Plaintext and code-context insertion expose different syntax boundaries. Engine identification requires controlled evidence, not one ambiguous marker.
Available globals, helpers, loaders, and sandbox policy determine reachable operations and impact.
Look for dynamic template construction or compilation rather than ordinary fixed-template data binding.
SSTI.exercise: Complete an introductory Academy SSTI lab or compare fixed-template binding with unsafe template concatenation in a local engine.
SSTI.quick: A harmless arithmetic marker such as `{{7*7}}` can distinguish data from evaluation in some engines; syntax and results are engine-dependent.
SSTI.risk: The application must compile/evaluate attacker-influenced source; impact ranges from output manipulation to capabilities exposed by the engine runtime.
SSTI.test: Supply arithmetic syntax as a data value and verify the fixed renderer displays it literally rather than evaluating it.
SSTI.defense: Keep templates trusted and static, pass data separately, constrain loaders/helpers, and avoid untrusted compilation. Monitor template errors and unexpected dynamic-source creation.
SSTI.gotcha: HTML escaping addresses output interpretation, not server-side evaluation. A sandbox is not a universal guarantee against unsafe exposed helpers.

Insecure Deserialization.model: Deserializing untrusted object graphs can invoke constructors, callbacks, or type-specific behavior that the application did not intend to authorize.
concepts: Native object formats, polymorphic type metadata, and unsafe YAML loaders differ from simple schema-validated data formats.
Gadget behavior depends on exact libraries, versions, and reachable types; a published gadget chain is not universal.
Trace serialized bytes to object construction and subsequent method calls, including signed-but-overprivileged internal messages.
Insecure Deserialization.exercise: Use a toy serializable class whose callback only writes a local marker, then replace object deserialization with a strict data schema. Compare behavior without using real exploit chains.
Insecure Deserialization.quick: Prefer data-only formats and explicit schemas; reject arbitrary type selection. Integrity checks do not justify accepting unnecessarily powerful object graphs.
Insecure Deserialization.risk: Reachable constructors/callbacks execute with the consumer's authority; impact depends on available types and downstream use.
Insecure Deserialization.test: Submit unapproved type metadata to the protected toy consumer and verify rejection before any marker callback runs.
Insecure Deserialization.defense: Avoid native object deserialization for untrusted data, allowlist required types, patch dependencies, and constrain resource use. Monitor type/parse failures and unexpected side effects.
